Part 12 Conditional Foresight and Bounded Choice ​

Projection unfolds conditions and paths. Conditional foresight goes further by making judgments about the future that can fail. Bounded choice compares what can be done, how to do it, when to stop, and when to refrain within the bounds of values, protection, and authorization. This Part places foresight and choice together to form a closed loop of work. Their separate contracts[1] prevent “a consequence was predicted” from being taken to mean “there is therefore authority to make others take on an action.” Comparing and recommending options are analytical outputs and can be completed when normative premises and constraints are clear. Real-world adoption and execution must separately undergo the applicable protection, review, and authorization procedures.

12Note

Understanding this section

Part XII: Conditional Foresight and Bounded Choice

The previous part mapped possible paths; this part asks which future judgments will submit to tests at resolution, and under which values and protective conditions actions may be compared and recommended. These questions connect, but prediction confers no power to make others bear costs.

Conditional foresight undertakes fallible future judgments within targets, deadlines, and evidence boundaries. Fallibility requires explicit support, non-support, or unresolved conditions at resolution; not every path may count as success, and deadlines cannot extend indefinitely. Sections 12.2–12.7 specify registration, local predictability, baselines, expression, evaluation, and failure semantics.

Bounded choice compares what can be done, how, when to stop, and when not to act within explicit value, protection, and authorization boundaries. Section 12.8 onward connects foresight to options, distributional consequences, reversibility, and procedures for actual adoption. Inaction also requires comparison and cannot be presumed costless.

Together they form a working loop: predictions provide conditional consequences for choices; actions and responses may change future material; outcomes then help correct judgments. Separate contracts prevent cross-level substitution: a likely consequence does not mean it ought to be produced, or that anyone may compel others to bear costs to avoid it.

A comparative recommendation may itself be a complete analytical deliverable. With explicit evidence, normative premises, costs, and limits, grounded preferences, rejection, or delay recommendations are possible; lack of execution authority need not reduce the output to questions alone. Actual adoption and execution separately require applicable protection, review, and valid authorization. “Only advice” also cannot conceal foreseeable high-impact uses.

This part promises neither universal predictability nor a model that unifies every value. It permits bounded answers, unknowns, incomparability, multiple options, and current nonaction, requiring explicit material that could change the judgment.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Turn a judgment about the future into a foresight contract with a target, deadline, and evaluation obligations.

  2. 2

    Separately disclose the normative, protective, distributional, and permission conditions for comparing options.

  3. 3

    Allow complete recommendations for deliberation, without turning predictions or recommendations into execution permission.

  4. 4

    Append actual outcomes as feedback records while retaining the original contract and failure records.

Distinctions to keep clear

Conditional foresight

Undertakes a fallible judgment about a future target.

≠

Bounded choice

Compares options under explicit norms and limits.

Recommendation for deliberation

It can be an explicit analytical conclusion.

≠

Actual adoption

Must independently pass the applicable protection, review, and authorization requirements.

Teaching construction: the same prediction is insufficient to determine an actionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe numbers, objects, and consequences are teaching stipulations; no actual measurements or population trials were conducted.

A fictional task predicts that a queueing arrangement will reduce average waiting by 2 minutes, but it is unknown whether it makes one person unable to exit wait an extra hour. This average foresight can enter a comparison but cannot determine that the arrangement should be executed. Distribution, minimum protections, alternatives, and permissions must be explicit. Even if the completed analysis favors it, the real queue has not thereby been scheduled.

BoundaryThis does not provide operational advice to actual service organizations.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe model predicts overall improvement, so it can directly order everyone to adopt the option.

What it limitsFactual consequences do not automatically generate value premises, rights-based justification, or execution permission.

12.1Keeping the Four Outputs Separate ​

In brief“I think this will happen, so that should be done” may quietly cross several gates. This section requires identifying whether we are explaining the past, unfolding conditions, predicting the future, or proposing a normative choice: each answers to different questions.
Codes used in this section (1)
  • C12Check on the Validity of Normative Bridging

Explanation, projection, conditional foresight, and bounded choice must be labeled separately.

OutputCore QuestionRequired InputsOutput Ceiling
ExplanationWhat has happened, and why might it have happened?Object, scale, evidence, mechanism, and counterexamplesAn account of the mechanism within stated limits
ProjectionWhich paths could unfold after a condition or event?Frozen snapshot, update rules, clocks, and branchesConditional paths and signals that distinguish them
Conditional foresightFor the stated target and horizon, which path is better supported as an expectation?Registration before results, a simple baseline, metrics, and write-backA judgment that can be calibrated and can fail
Bounded choiceCompare and recommend options under explicit normative premises. Real-world adoption separately undergoes protection, review, and authorizationAnalysis requires normative premises, evidence, options, costs, and the people affected. Real-world adoption also requires N, PF, J, O, and C12A refutable analytical recommendation or an authorized record of bounded choice, with their statuses kept separate

Explanation can generate candidates for projection, but it cannot automatically establish what will happen. Projection can generate candidate forecasts, but it cannot count every path as a success. Foresight can inform comparisons between options, but it cannot automatically generate values or authority. Even a bounded choice that passes its checks does not guarantee successful execution in reality. Stopping, rollback, and outcome write-back are still required.

12.1Note

Understanding this section

12.1 Separating four types of output

“I think this will happen, so that should be done” may quietly cross several gates. This section requires identifying whether we are explaining the past, unfolding conditions, predicting the future, or proposing a normative choice: each answers to different questions.

Explanation answers what happened and why it may have happened, requiring objects, scales, evidence, mechanisms, and counterexamples. Its upper bound is a bounded mechanistic account. A coherent account of the past does not prove that the future will unfold the same way. An explanation may also retain several mechanisms; unknowns cannot be narrated as a unique cause.

Projection starts from a frozen snapshot, update rules, clocks, and branches to provide conditional paths and distinguishing signals. It can say, “if working-time and resource conditions remain, this branch may unfold.” Listing multiple paths does not give each a probability, and selecting the realized branch after the fact cannot establish predictive success for the entire projection.

Conditional foresight adds registration before the outcome, a simple baseline, target indicators, and feedback-record obligations. It asks which path is better supported as an expectation within a specified deadline. Its expression may be an evidence-based probability, ranking, or direction, or remain unknown when evidence is insufficient. Being open to calibration and failure is not the same as having demonstrated excellent calibration; the two cannot be merged into a single “reliable” label.

Bounded-choice analysis requires normative premises, evidence, genuinely comparable options, prices to be paid, and affected parties. Real-world adoption separately requires N explicit norms, PF protection floor, J jurisdictional authorization, O1–O4 processes, and C12 bridging qualifications. This invokes the source text's division of work; it is not a model inventing public authority. Even when these premises remain unmet, explicit analysis for deliberation is possible, but it must not claim to be ready for execution.

Connecting successive gates does not automatically upgrade status: explanation generates projection candidates; projection generates foresight candidates; foresight supplies consequences for comparison; norms and procedures support bounded choice; actual execution still requires stopping, rollback, and feedback records. Any layer with sufficient material can provide a clear bounded answer. Answering an explanatory question does not require completing every action procedure.

A single deliverable can contain all four output types, but their status must be labeled by sentence or paragraph, with sources and support ceilings stated separately. For example, discovering a processing-capacity decline after the fact is explanatory material; assuming continued low speed tomorrow is a scenario; registering the probability that tomorrow's 09:00 backlog exceeds a threshold is foresight; recommending maintenance first is normative analysis. They can share material without sharing all qualifications.

Accuracy is performance relative to a target and evaluation contract, not a moral, legal, or representative qualification. A weather model's smaller positional error does not authorize its publisher to determine how anyone evacuates. Real-world protective action has its own actors, permissions, and procedures. This non-entailment does not deny weather prediction's usefulness; it prevents usefulness from expanding into unlimited power.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    State separately each output type's question, inputs, and supportable conclusions.

  2. 2

    Check what additional evidential or normative conditions are needed to move from one layer to the next.

  3. 3

    Evaluate foresight only against its frozen target and deadline; do not count all scenario branches as successes.

  4. 4

    Analytical recommendations state norms and distribution; real-world adoption separately checks N/PF/J/O/C12.

  5. 5

    Retain responsibility for failure, stopping, and remedies after execution; a qualified procedure does not guarantee success.

Distinctions to keep clear

Explanation

Provides a bounded mechanistic account of phenomena that have occurred.

≠

Projection

Unfolds possible paths from conditions.

Projection candidate

Lists consequences if assumptions hold.

≠

Registered foresight

Frozen before the outcome and subject to evaluation at the deadline.

Evaluable

A target and scoring contract are in place.

≠

Good performance has been verified

Requires actual outcomes and appropriate review.

Foresight ranking

An evidential judgment that a consequence is more reasonably expected.

≠

Recommendation ranking

Also requires norms, distribution, costs, and protection.

Bounded choice passes

The relevant contract is supported.

≠

Execution is certain to succeed

Real-world deviations still require stopping and feedback records.

Teaching construction: assigning four statements to their proper placesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe entire example is a teaching structure and supplies no real-world probability; yesterday's records are also constructed stipulations.

Fictional records show 2 arrivals yesterday, 1 completion, and a starting value of 6. Under the assumption of no other flows, the endpoint is 7: a conditional explanation of records of past events. If the same conditions hold tomorrow, the endpoint will increase by another 1: a projection. Conditional foresight requires freezing, before the outcome, the target “whether it exceeds 7 tomorrow at 09:00,” the information cutoff, baseline, scoring, and signals, and giving an evidence-based judgment. If the stated norms are safeguarding deadlines and respecting personnel's minimum protections, and a recommendation follows comparison of maintenance, delay, transfer, and inaction, this is bounded-choice analysis. It still does not mean maintenance has been authorized or completed.

BoundaryCorrect arithmetic does not prove an actual mechanism. Without actual registration and outcomes, no foresight gain can be claimed.

Mathematical construction: likelihood and preference can rank in opposite directionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe probabilities and values are purely constructed; no real-world event risk was estimated.

Fictional events A and B have probabilities 0.8 and 0.2, stipulated by the example. The value premise considers A seriously harmful and B harmless. A's greater likelihood does not mean it should be promoted; it may instead be something against which protection is warranted. If a response harms third parties, rights and distribution require separate comparison; 0.8 alone cannot determine coercive measures.

BoundaryNo specific action follows, nor is expected benefit treated as the only norm.

2024 North Atlantic cyclone forecasts: the boundary of an evaluation metricDocumented case

The North Atlantic table in the UK Met Office's 2024 Northern Hemisphere cyclone verification report lists a T+24-hour mean direct positional error of 57 km. This specific evaluation metric is evidence about predictive performance. The lesson uses it to show that the metric itself contains no authorization to direct particular people's actions.

12.2Conditional Forecast Registration ​

In briefFirst specify what counts as the prediction, when it ends, and how correctness is judged, then await the result. Otherwise, “the relationship will improve” can forever mean a slight improvement somewhere, and no model can genuinely fail.

Each forecast is frozen after the input cutoff and before the results appear. The minimum fields include forecast ID, model version, target, horizon, scope of objects and circles[2], baseline time, input cutoff, simple baseline, candidate mechanisms, set of paths, probability or ranking expression, calibration plan, decision threshold, early signals, contrary signals, suspension conditions, retirement conditions, outcome write-back, registration time, and evidence references. Include the decision threshold when it is used for the corresponding decision. Otherwise mark it not applicable.

The target must be decidable. For example, “the relationship will improve” must specify which observables change within a stated window, who observes them, what threshold applies, and what outcomes count as unresolved. The horizon can be a window. There is no need to fabricate a precise date. The scope of the objects and circles must be frozen to avoid narrowing it to the successful subgroup after results appear.

Registration ItemMinimum QuestionBias It Prevents
TargetWhen the horizon ends, how will we know whether it occurred, did not occur, or cannot be determined?Vague success criteria
HorizonWhen does the window start and end, and when does input collection stop?Waiting indefinitely
Simple baselineWhat is the comparison prediction without multi-circle mechanisms?Letting a complex story win by its own standards
PathsWhich paths are mutually exclusive, parallel, or incomparable?Post hoc selection
ExpressionProbability, interval, level, or direction alone?False precision
SignalsWhat would strengthen or weaken support for a path?Looking only for supporting evidence
Write-backWhat is the source of the outcome, and when is it appended?Letting failures disappear
12.2Note

Understanding this section

12.2 Registering conditional foresight

First specify what counts as the prediction, when it ends, and how correctness is judged, then await the result. Otherwise, “the relationship will improve” can forever mean a slight improvement somewhere, and no model can genuinely fail.

Registration time, input cutoff, and target deadline play three different roles. First close the entry point for material usable in this run, then freeze the judgment, without having already seen the target outcome. The deadline may be a window; the input cutoff need not equal the target's start. Late evidence can inform a new version but cannot backfill the old run. If the target outcome is already known, the work is retrospective explanation or backtesting and cannot be renamed foresight registration.

The foresight ID and model version ensure traceability. The target, deadline, object, and circle scope determine who and what will be evaluated at the deadline; the baseline time specifies the starting point for measuring change. If the original target covers the whole team, narrowing it after the outcome to high-performing members changes the contract and cannot retain the original success status.

The target must be adjudicable, specifying at least the observable quantity, observer or source, threshold, and treatment of missingness. For example, if “relationship improvement” uses a particular scale, it evaluates only change under that measurement contract, not whether the whole relationship or everyone's life improved. First check whether the target definition actually corresponds to the task; do not replace the outcome the user cares about merely to make scoring easier.

A simple baseline prevents complex stories from declaring their own victory. The candidate mechanisms and path set specify mutual exclusivity, parallelism, or incomparability. Probabilities, intervals, grades, or directions must match the strength of their grounds. Without grounds for ranking, state unknown; mandatory registration does not justify invented numbers. Fill in decision thresholds only when used for decisions; otherwise they may be marked not applicable with a reason.

Early and contrary signals provide material for distinguishing paths. Suspension conditions specify when to stop using a model or variable; retirement conditions specify when to withdraw it. Calibration and outcome-feedback plans specify the actual labels, timing of appended records, and evaluation rules. A single prediction's score is not long-term calibration; the plan must also specify consistent conventions and uncertainty handling across accumulated tasks.

The original table's seven minimum questions address vague success, endless waiting, complexity as self-proof, retrospective branch selection, false precision, seeking support alone, and disappearing failures. A filled table is not a certificate of immunity to failure. Honest unknowns in its fields may also mean the entry is not yet qualified for release as foresight.

Subsection 12.2.1 bounds local capability claims by object, scale, resources, and expression; 12.2.2 requires independent evaluation of each recursive order. The parent section governs registration entry. One overall prediction ID cannot combine results from different orders, populations, or cutoffs as a single item.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Before the outcome, freeze the target, deadline, scope, input cutoff, registration time, and version.

  2. 2

    Define adjudicable rules for occurred/did not occur/unresolved to prevent changing populations and thresholds after the outcome.

  3. 3

    Fix the simple baseline, mechanistic paths, expression form, and applicable decision thresholds.

  4. 4

    Specify positive and contrary signals, suspension, retirement, calibration, and append-only outcome feedback in advance.

  5. 5

    When material is insufficient, retain the gaps preventing publication; do not substitute empty forms or fabricated parameters.

Distinctions to keep clear

Input cutoff

The latest acquisition boundary for material allowed in this run.

≠

Outcome deadline

The time point or window at which the target is adjudicated.

Baseline time

The starting time for calculating change.

≠

Simple baseline model

A comparison judgment without complex structure.

Decision threshold

A trigger criterion for reviewing a specified action.

≠

Probability or classification expression

Does not automatically become execution permission and need not involve a decision.

Complete registration

Traceability and conditions for failure are explicit.

≠

Predictive capability established

Still requires outcomes, baselines, and appropriate evaluation.

Mathematical teaching construction: one complete foresight registrationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsProbabilities are a stipulated formal generating distribution, not estimates from actual repair data. All times, records, and calibration plans are constructed; repeated tasks were not actually conducted.

ID=Ptoy01, model v1; object=fictional repair queue Q, circles=no circle grouping used for this local task; baseline 08:00 B0=6; input cutoff 08:00, registration 08:01; target is recorded B≥8 at 10:00, horizon ending at that day's 10:00 count, labels verified at 10:05, with missing counts unresolved. Stipulated generating mechanism: arrivals 2/hour for two hours, processing rate c constant throughout, c=1 with probability 0.6 and c=3 with probability 0.4; endpoints are thus 8 or 4, target probability 0.6. Simple baseline p0=0.5 is an independently predefined teaching comparator. Paths are mutually exclusive; calibration plan accumulates tasks under the same mechanism and records Brier scores and event frequencies in equal-probability groups, without certifying calibration from one case. Decision threshold is inapplicable because only prediction is evaluated. Early signal=09:00 backlog 7 or 5 under the same definition; contrary signal=inconsistent values or changed generating conditions; suspension=changed input definition or object; retirement=long-term failure to outperform the baseline in later same-contract tests, after review. Write-back=append count source, label, loss, and deviations after 10:05; evidence reference=public stipulation Etoy in this example, not a real record.

BoundaryUsing the new 09:00 signal for updating requires a new frozen run; Ptoy01 remains evaluated on 08:00 information.

Teaching construction: operationalizing a vague target must preserve unresolved statusTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDesign principles only, without a real psychological test or personal-data collection. No threshold or scale is supplied, so no values are assigned.

“Team relationships improve” may be operationalized for a particular measurement task as “the same voluntary measurement on a fixed member set at two predefined times, using predefined scoring and missingness rules, with an indicator change reaching a threshold.” If members exit or refuse disclosure, do not default to improvement or deterioration; register missing/unresolved under prior rules and check target identity.

BoundaryOne indicator does not represent every relationship, dignity, or life outcome; real adoption requires construct and protection checks.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe original forecast concerned improvement across a department; looking only at an improved subgroup afterward also counts as success.

What it limitsObject scope has been switched; create a new target while continuing the old record.

Teaching counterexampleEven without real probability grounds, enter 0.5 to be neutral.

What it limits0.5 is a probability claim, not an automatic product of ignorance.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • A successful subgroup narrowed after the outcome must not count as a hit on the original target.
  • A window may be an interval, but it cannot be extended indefinitely after the fact.
  • Changes to target conventions require a new version; unresolved must not be entered as did not occur.

Scope and open questions

This section requires complete prior registration. The historical retrospective evaluation report obtained lacks this lesson's full frozen fields, so an explicit generating distribution and complete construction are used rather than presenting a retrospective report as prior registration.

  • No real forecast registration or experimental outcomes are provided here; a team-relationship task would additionally need suitable measurement, missingness rules, and protections.

12.2.1Limits of Local Predictability ​

In briefDo not ask only “can this model predict?” Ask which object, which state region, how far ahead, what error is allowed, and with what information and resources. Good performance on one task is not a license for every future.

Every predictability claim must specify its object, state region, scale and circles, time window, allowable error, available information, computing and observation resources, model version, baseline, abstention conditions, and failure conditions. This framework cannot directly answer whether the world as a whole is predictable. It can test only whether a particular task gains a limited increment within explicit bounds.

Classifications, levels, intervals, and probabilities carry different responsibilities for measurement and expression. They do not form a ladder of precision that every task has to climb. The chosen form of expression must be supported by the target, units, generation method, identification conditions, and calibration status. If there is no basis even for a qualitative direction, retain it as unknown. Direction is not the default when probability is unavailable. For known probabilities in formal models and for empirical probabilities, state the assumptions and limits of extrapolation separately. Text patterns and AI must not be used to invent real-world parameters. When citing an existing mathematical or physical theory, also register its original object, assumptions, mathematical limits or scaling laws, error, domain of validity, object mapping, counterexamples, and exit conditions. Borrowing the form of its equations alone is insufficient.

12.2.1Note

Understanding this section

12.2.1 Boundaries of local predictability

Do not ask only “can this model predict?” Ask which object, which state region, how far ahead, what error is allowed, and with what information and resources. Good performance on one task is not a license for every future.

Local predictability binds at least object, state region, scale and circles, window, tolerance, available information, computation and observation resources, version, baseline, abstention, and failure conditions. A model effective one hour ahead under normal load need not work under extreme load or a year ahead; expanding boundaries needs new evidence.

Predictability of the world as a whole exceeds this framework's directly testable scope. What is permitted here is bounded increment within particular tasks: local success does not establish complete foreknowledge, and long-term unknowns do not negate all short-window questions. Bounded capability may genuinely exist under its corresponding constraints.

Classification, ranking, intervals, and probability have different meanings. Classification identifies categories; ranking gives grounded order; intervals preserve admissible values or explicit coverage contracts; probability concerns event generation or empirical estimation. They are not a universal ladder from low to high. A task may need only a category, and probability need not suit the use better than a correct interval.

Choose expression after checking target, units, generating method, identification conditions, and calibration status. If even direction is unidentified, state unknown rather than “at least judge the trend.” A formal model may have known probabilities, explicitly supplied by assumptions; empirical probabilities need real data and applicable scope, not AI converting sparse prose into parameters.

Borrowing mathematical or physical theory also requires its original object, assumptions, limits or scaling laws, error, effective domain, object mapping, counterexamples, and exit conditions. Calling a community a fluid or information energy does not automatically apply the equations. Metaphors can prompt questions; quantitative laws require real mappings and validation.

Resource limits are part of capability. Backtesting with material available only later does not establish real-time predictability then; computation exceeding the decision window may prevent delivering the claimed lead time. Abstention preserves the ability to withhold judgments outside the applicable domain. Report abstention scope in evaluation rather than showing only easy cases the model answers.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Bound predictability claims to specific objects, state regions, windows, tolerances, and resources.

  2. 2

    Declare information cutoff, version, baseline, and abstention/failure conditions.

  3. 3

    Choose expression by target and evidence; direction is not an evidence-free default.

  4. 4

    For borrowed formulas, check original assumptions and object mappings, stating error and exit conditions.

  5. 5

    Downgrade or retest out-of-boundary results; do not extrapolate automatically from local to global.

Distinctions to keep clear

Bounded task increment

Outperforms the baseline under explicit boundaries.

≠

The whole world is predictable

Does not follow from local evaluation.

Formally known probability

Given by a public model or stipulation.

≠

Empirical probability

Needs real material and calibration; the two must not be switched.

Directional judgment

Requires an identifiable sign or ordering.

≠

Arbitrarily stating a trend without probabilities

Also exceeds evidence boundaries.

Similar-looking formulas

A metaphor or heuristic lead.

≠

Valid quantitative mapping

Requires objects, units, assumptions, and empirical support.

Mathematical construction: no probability may also mean no directionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe admissible mechanism set is constructed, not claimed to exhaust all real possibilities.

Suppose compatible mechanisms give future change Δ as −2 or +3, without probabilities or evidence selecting a mechanism. Report set {−2,+3}, not “tends upward,” nor average 0.5 as a real prediction. Only new evidence excluding the negative branch permits a positive direction within the remaining models.

BoundaryA conditional set differs from a confidence interval; no equal branch probabilities are assigned.

Mathematical construction: different tolerances produce different task eligibilityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsNumbers and tolerances are teaching stipulations; one case establishes no long-term capability.

A fictional point prediction is 10, actual value 12, absolute error 2. It meets a prior task tolerance ≤3 but fails another task's tolerance ≤1. Success on the former cannot transfer to the latter, nor may tolerance change from 1 to 3 after the outcome.

BoundaryTolerance must also suit actual use and harm, not be widened arbitrarily for better scores.

12.2.2Evaluation of Recursive Foresight by Order ​

In briefA correct first order and incorrect third order cannot be blended into an attractive total and called “effective recursion.” Each order has different questions and informational dependencies, requiring separate freezing and comparison with reasonable shallower methods.

Freeze and evaluate the first, second, and third orders separately. They must not be combined into a single overall hit rate. Each order must be compared with state continuation without further recursion, a direct longer-horizon judgment, and a shallower order followed by simple continuation. If going to the third order adds only narrative without stable out-of-sample gains, it may be retained as an exploratory scenario. It does not qualify as evidence of foresight capability.

Without new external material, the source lineage of every child run still ends at the same frozen starting point. Post-processing can add reasoning within the model and reveal sensitivity and hidden consequences. It cannot manufacture evidence about reality. When actual intermediate outcomes arrive, a new frozen run should be created and compared with the original recursive paths. The outcomes must not be fed back into the old paths.

12.2.2Note

Understanding this section

12.2.2 Evaluation of recursive foresight by order

A correct first order and incorrect third order cannot be blended into an attractive total and called “effective recursion.” Each order has different questions and informational dependencies, requiring separate freezing and comparison with reasonable shallower methods.

Register object, target, horizon, input cutoff, expression, and evaluation rules separately for first, second, and third orders. If they predict different targets, adding hits into an opaque total rate is invalid. Any combined metric needs its own prior definition and weights while retaining order-specific performance; it cannot replace original contracts.

Each order needs three comparators: state continuation without further recursion; direct judgment of the same distant target; and a shallower order plus simple continuation. These distinguish genuine need for reentry structure from mere passage of time. Comparing second-order errors on a difficult distant target directly with an easy first-order short-term target cannot establish recursion as harmful or beneficial.

Fair comparison matches target, horizon, available information, and evaluation rules, with a reasonable account of computation and tuning opportunities. Extra evidence, computation, and richer structure can each generate gain and should be distinguished as far as possible. A simple baseline need not be artificially made as large as the complex system, nor deliberately denied available information.

Without new external material, every child run's evidence lineage still returns to the same frozen starting point. Postprocessing may reveal previously underived logical consequences, sensitivities, or hidden conditions—a real inferential increment—but does not add a real sample or independent evidence source.

When actual intermediate outcomes arrive, create a new-cutoff run. Compare “projecting all the way from the original start” with “updating using later actual conditions,” but the latter uses more material. Gains cannot all be credited to recursion, nor fed backward into old paths to make them perpetually correct.

If three orders add only stories without stable out-of-sample increment, retain exploratory scenarios without foresight-capability eligibility. One better or worse performance establishes no universal rule. Judge stability within registered use and independent evaluation scope, narrowing windows or retiring when necessary.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Freeze target, window, information, and scoring contract separately for each order.

  2. 2

    Compare the same target against state continuation, direct distant judgment, and shallow-order continuation.

  3. 3

    Distinguish differences in information, computation, and structure, preserving order-specific scores.

  4. 4

    Child runs without new external material do not increase real-evidence counts.

  5. 5

    Create new runs for intermediate actual conditions; without stable gain, downgrade to exploratory scenarios.

Distinctions to keep clear

Evaluation by order

Score each order's own task against reasonable comparators separately.

≠

Overall hit rate

May conceal differences in task difficulty, horizon, and failure.

Internal inferential increment

Reveals consequences implied by original inputs.

≠

External evidential increment

New real material appears, with different status.

Prediction updated with actual conditions

Reestimated using a new cutoff.

≠

Original recursive prediction

Uses only the old starting point and remains under its old contract.

Direct distant-target comparison

Prediction for the same target without reentry.

≠

First-order short-term score

A different task cannot directly rank methods.

Mathematical construction: recursion does not beat baselines on the same targetTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll four predictions, the label, and the rule are teaching constructions, not a real experiment; all comparisons concern the same hour-3 target.

A fictional third-order target is the hour-3 queue value, actual label 10. Predictions are recursive 14, direct distant-target 11, current-state continuation 12, and shallower-plus-continuation 10. Under predefined absolute error, scores are 4,1,2,0. This instance does not support recursive superiority; a correct first-order answer to a different short-term task cannot offset the third-order error.

BoundaryOne sample cannot establish that every recursive method is worse; it gives only this instance's bounded comparison.

Teaching construction: new actual conditions cannot leak backward into old ordersTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTimes and data flow are constructed; no real forecasting system was run.

Suppose three-order predictions are frozen at 08:00 and a new count arrives at 09:00. A new run from that count may improve the 10:00 prediction, and the updated result can be reported while retaining the 08:00 forecast. Writing the 09:00 value into the old first order, recomputing old second and third orders, and claiming “predicted at 08:00” is information leakage.

BoundaryAn update's value does not make the old run valueless; evaluate the two information sets separately.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleGenerating 100 child runs from one starting point equals 100 independent observations.

What it limitsThe source lineage is shared; more computation adds no real samples.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThe first order is accurate and the third inaccurate; averaging proves overall three-order effectiveness.

What it limitsTasks and horizons differ by order; retain separate scores and same-target comparisons.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not count regenerated child texts as independent samples.
  • Out-of-sample evaluation also needs protection against target, time, and source leakage.
  • Exploratory scenarios may be useful even without supported foresight gain.

Scope and open questions

This section specifies evaluation by order and information lineage. No actual archive of frozen third-order predictions and independent labels exists here; reproducible scoring for the same target avoids inventing a recursive-foresight experiment.

  • Stable out-of-sample gains require actual records by order and same-target controls, which this lesson has not implemented.

    Can improvement from new intermediate actual conditions be attributed entirely to recursion?

  3. 3

    Is postprocessing without new observations entirely valueless?

Third order 14, direct 11, continuation 12, shallow-plus-continuation 10, label 10: what are their errors?

4,1,2,0. Recursion does not dominate here, without a universal long-term judgment.

Can improvement from new intermediate actual conditions be attributed entirely to recursion?

No. It adds information; use a new version and distinguish informational from structural contributions.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Is postprocessing without new observations entirely valueless?

It may add reasoning, sensitivity analysis, and conditional understanding, but real-world evidence does not grow by itself.

12.3Simple Baselines and Incremental Capability ​

In briefA complex model must answer a plain question: with the same information, target, and cutoff, what would a simpler method do? Richer stories, more diagrams, or more variables cannot replace that comparison.

A multi-circle model claimed to improve foresight must be compared with simple models suited to the task and with existing methods in the domain under the same information, cutoff, target, and evaluation rules. Make the comparison materials, inference budgets, and opportunities for tuning as comparable as possible. State separately what is contributed by additional information, additional computation, and additional structural assumptions. A simple baseline need not be artificially enlarged to match the size of the complex model. Predictive systems generally require independent testing or out-of-sample review. If neither can be obtained, explicitly retain the status that the capability has yet to be established.

Common baselines include continuing the current trend, carrying forward the most recent state, using historical frequencies, using only the actor state, using only the primary circle state, and using an existing model in the domain. Comparisons should use the same target, horizon, data cutoff, and evaluation metrics. If a complex model improves explanation but does not improve prediction, record the outcome as “a gain in explanation is present, and a gain in foresight is not supported.”

Model complexity also has costs. More variables increase missing data, measurement error, privacy risk, overfitting, and maintenance debt. If a multi-circle model works in only a few cases, its domain of application should be restricted. If gains disappear over time, it should be downgraded or retired. If the simple baseline performs equally well, it should be preferred.

12.3Note

Understanding this section

12.3 Simple baselines and incremental capability

A complex model must answer a plain question: with the same information, target, and cutoff, what would a simpler method do? Richer stories, more diagrams, or more variables cannot replace that comparison.

Incremental capability is a difference relative to a task-appropriate baseline, not an attractive error figure reported by the model alone. A baseline may extend a trend, retain the most recent state, use historical frequencies, use only agent state or the main circle's state, or adopt an established domain method. Selection should fit the data and task, without deliberately choosing an obviously unsuitable weak opponent.

Fair comparison first requires the same information, cutoff, target, horizon, and evaluation rules. If the complex model receives later events while the simple model uses only earlier materials, the difference cannot be attributed to multi-circle structure. If the complex model is scored only on easy samples while the baseline is scored on the whole set, that is not the same comparison either.

Materials, reasoning budgets, and tuning opportunities should be as proportionate as possible, without forcing a simple baseline to become a complex model. Explain separately the contributions of added information, computation, and structural assumptions. Restricted controls or ablations may help, but one overall score cannot complete causal attribution. State honestly when contributions cannot be isolated.

Predictive systems usually require independent testing or out-of-sample review, with protection against temporal, object, or source leakage. In time series, future materials cannot enter past prediction inputs, and related records should not be treated as fully independent samples. Without available tests, retain capability as unestablished; training fit or retrospective explanation cannot count as foresight performance.

Separate explanatory gain from predictive gain. A model may clarify mechanisms, cost-bearing positions, or constraints without predicting better than the baseline; if that explanatory gain has corresponding materials, retain it while stating that foresight gain is unsupported. Whether explanation actually improves also needs criteria; longer text cannot certify itself.

Complexity carries costs of missingness, mismeasurement, privacy, overfitting, and maintenance. Collecting more people's information adds risks, and model versions need continuing maintenance. Limit use if effectiveness holds only in a small state domain; downgrade or retire when gains decline; if performance is equal and no other sufficient reason exists, prefer the simpler model rather than paying needless costs for a larger terminology.

Equal performance is a bounded conclusion about the current comparison and need not establish population-level statistical equivalence. One win for a simple method does not mean complex methods are always worse; one win for a complex method does not establish universal superiority either. The final report should state samples, error uncertainty, applicability domain, tuning opportunities, and costs, not merely name a winner.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Choose a task-appropriate simple or domain baseline and freeze the comparison contract first.

  2. 2

    Give methods the same target, information cutoff, horizon, samples, and scoring.

  3. 3

    Reasonably balance computation and tuning, separating information, computational, and structural contributions.

  4. 4

    Test with independent or out-of-sample materials; without them, capability remains unestablished.

  5. 5

    Limit the applicability domain by gains and costs, downgrade when gains disappear, and prefer simplicity under equal performance.

Distinctions to keep clear

Explanatory gain

Evidence-backed improvement in understanding mechanisms or constraints.

≠

Foresight gain

Better performance on unseen outcomes under the same contract.

Fair computational conditions

Comparable budgets and tuning opportunities, with differences transparent.

≠

Equal-sized baseline

A simple method need not expand to the same scale.

Added information

Richer or newer inputs.

≠

Structural increment

A difference from representations and mechanisms under corresponding information conditions.

Training fit

Explains records already used for tuning.

≠

Out-of-sample performance

Evaluation on materials not used for model selection, still requiring leakage prevention.

Skill relative to a baseline

Improvement in a loss relative to the comparator.

≠

Event probability or hit rate

Different quantities; percentage signs do not make them interchangeable.

Mathematical construction: comparing average errors for the same targetTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll data and their independent status are teaching stipulations; no actual test was performed.

Fictional independent test labels are y=(10,12,8), complex-model predictions (9,13,9), and simple-model predictions (10,10,10). Under the predetermined mean absolute error, the complex model has (1+1+1)/3=1 and the simple model (0+2+2)/3=4/3. On this test set the complex method's average error is lower by 1/3; if collection costs also exist, the net choice still requires normative comparison. These three samples alone cannot establish a stable advantage across the entire domain.

BoundaryError improvement holds only for this sample and metric, not in place of confidence intervals or tests of long-term gain.

Mathematical construction: a skill percentage is not a hit rateTeaching scenario

AssumptionsLoss units are consistent, the baseline is nonzero, and the skill definition is this example's publicly stated rule.

In a teaching task, the baseline's average loss is 10 and the model's 8. Define relative skill S=1−L模型/L基线 (S = 1 − model loss/baseline loss), giving S=1−8/10=0.2, or 20%. This means loss is 20% lower than the baseline in this example, not that the event has probability 20% or that 80% or 20% of predictions hit individually.

BoundaryDifferent domains may use different skill scores; this formula cannot be forced onto every report.

Teaching construction: later information creates an unfair winTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTimes, information, and performance are a teaching scenario, with no actual operational data.

Fictional A predicts 10:00 inventory at 08:00 using only 08:00 materials; B predicts the same target at 09:30 after seeing most incoming stock and has lower error. One may say B made a later prediction with more information, not that B's structural model is stronger under the same cutoff. Compare separately using common 08:00 or common 09:30 materials.

BoundaryLater updating may be useful, but remaining lead time, the decision window, and information costs require separate evaluation.

The 2024 North Atlantic verification: skill requires a comparatorDocumented case

The Met Office reports North Atlantic T+24-hour Track skill of 68%; its official error definitions explain that this compares model position forecasts with the CLIPER climatology–persistence baseline, with positive values indicating lower model error. The added point here is that 68% is neither event probability nor case-by-case hit rate.

12.4Probability, Levels, and Time Windows ​

In briefProbability, priority for attention, personal belief, and greater value can all be expressed numerically, but are different quantities. Clarifying which question a number answers matters more than writing it with precision.

Where the evidence permits, one may give a probability or probability interval and state the model, prior, data, and grounds for calibration. When there is insufficient basis for a probability, one may give levels or compare paths to the extent supported by evidence. Sample size alone does not determine the type of output. When even the direction or ordering cannot be identified, explicitly retain it as unknown and identify observations that could distinguish the alternatives. Giving only the direction does not waive evidential responsibility. The strength of the expression depends on the evidence and use, independently of how much certainty the user wants.

Evidential StatusAppropriate ExpressionWhat Must Accompany It
A probability model or empirical estimate with clear grounds and a decidable targetProbability or probability intervalMethod of generation, prior if applicable, data, limits of applicability, and calibration status
Insufficient basis for probability, but grounds for path levels or orderingLevels of support or an orderingGrounds, incomparable items, and contrary signals
The direction can be identified, or it remains unknownA supported conditional direction, or an explicit unknownIdentification conditions, trigger points, minimal observation, and stopping conditions
Target or object is unstableWithhold the forecastThe contract that must be redefined

Time windows should match mechanism clocks. Immediate reactions can use a short window. Organizational or institutional changes require a longer one. Compressing a long-term mechanism into a short period can lead to a mistaken finding of no effect. Extrapolating a short-term signal indefinitely can lead to a mistaken finding of a trend. When several clocks coexist, separate horizons may be registered for different intermediate outcomes.

Real-world probabilities, actors’ subjective beliefs, decision weights, a model’s ordering of paths, and the allocation of computation at the next step are distinct quantities. A real-world probability must specify the target event and the basis for estimation or calibration. For a subjective belief, state who is judging, what information they have, and how they reached the judgment. Decision weights are interpreted according to the descriptive model or normative premises in use. Computational priorities specify why further investigation is worthwhile. Frequencies of branches obtained by taking more draws from a model must not be treated directly as real-world probabilities. The path most worth investigating or most hoped for must not be described as the most likely.

When probabilities cannot be determined reliably, a path may be investigated first because its consequences are severe, the response window is short, or it is easy to distinguish. Disclose the reason for the priority and the budget for investigating it, and retain the probability as unknown. Percentages must not be invented to establish an ordering. An action comparison still has to state normative objectives, distributional consequences, and feasible choices separately. An ordering by probability does not directly determine the order of recommendations.

Probabilities and levels have different meanings. A model’s conditional probability under given assumptions, uncertainty in an individual judgment, empirical calibration in a long series of repeated tasks, and normative priority must not use one number as though they referred to the same thing. A posterior can be obtained from a small sample and an explicit prior, but its real-world applicability still depends on the model. A large sample cannot repair an incorrect definition of what is observed. Without evidence, even the direction can remain unknown. Reducing the claim to direction alone does not automatically make it reliable. 〔Studies 03.04, 07.07〕

12.4Note

Understanding this section

12.4 Probabilities, grades, and time windows

Probability, priority for attention, personal belief, and greater value can all be expressed numerically, but are different quantities. Clarifying which question a number answers matters more than writing it with precision.

Probabilities or probability intervals must correspond to decidable events and specify the generative model, priors where applicable, data, boundaries, and calibration status. With insufficient probability grounds, evidence-backed grades or path comparisons may be given, but ranking itself may also be unknown; ‘no probability’ cannot automatically become ‘at least a direction can be given’. Sample size is only one condition and does not determine output type alone.

The source table's four evidence statuses have different ceilings: probability grounds permit probabilities; grade-only grounds require retaining incomparable items and contrary signals; direction is given only with identification grounds, otherwise unknown plus the minimum discriminating observation; unstable targets or objects prohibit issuing foresight until the contract is redefined. They are not a mandatory sequential downgrade ladder.

Time windows follow mechanism clocks; short-term emotional responses, organizational processes, and institutional changes cannot share one default horizon. Forcing a slow mechanism into a short window may wrongly judge ineffectiveness before it could take effect; extending short-term signals indefinitely mistakes transients for trends. Multiclock tasks may register separate horizons for intermediate and final outcomes while retaining their respective evaluations.

Real-world probability concerns event occurrence under corresponding conditions and needs estimation or calibration grounds; subjective belief records an agent's judgment under particular information; decision weights come from a descriptive model or value premises; path rankings hold only under their comparison relation; computational priorities state what limited resources should examine first. Even the same 0.8 across all five cannot make them prove one another.

High consequences, a short window, or easy discrimination may give a path with unknown probability high checking priority. Disclose priority reasons and budgets rather than invent a percentage to appear rational. Most worth checking does not mean most likely, and most desired does not mean most likely either; recommendation rankings additionally require norms and distributional considerations and do not follow directly from occurrence probabilities.

Model sampling frequencies are computational results under given parameters, sampling methods, and rules. They may estimate model-conditional probabilities, but real-world probabilities additionally require mappings, parameter support, and calibration. More samples cannot repair a wrong model or unobserved variables. If sampling deliberately oversamples a risk branch, its frequency may not even equal probability under the model's original distribution; preserve weights and methods.

A small sample can produce a posterior under explicit priors and likelihoods, but that posterior remains assumption-dependent; the small sample itself cannot certify real-world parameters. Large samples may also share incorrect definitions or selection bias; precise estimation of the wrong quantity is not the probability of the event being asked about.

Publish probability judgments, empirical calibration, and normative priorities separately. High personal confidence is not calibrated long-run frequency; good calibration on comparable tasks also does not automatically satisfy protections for every subgroup or action authorization. Strength of expression rests on evidence and use, not readers' desired certainty or model fluency.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Specify what each number or grade concerns: event probability, belief, weight, ranking, or research priority.

  2. 2

    Choose the expression according to target stability, generation method, and identification conditions; retain unknown if grounds for direction are absent.

  3. 3

    Set corresponding windows for each mechanism's outcomes rather than extrapolating short-term signals indefinitely.

  4. 4

    Distinguish model sampling from real-world probability, explaining boundaries of priors, data, selection, and calibration.

  5. 5

    High-risk checks may be prioritized without inventing probabilities; action recommendations require separate normative comparison.

Distinctions to keep clear

Real-world probability

Concerns the target event, conditions, and estimation grounds.

≠

Personal belief

A person's judgment under particular information, not automatically empirically calibrated.

Research priority

Affected by consequences, windows, discriminability, and budget.

≠

Ranking by occurrence probability

Requires corresponding evidence of event probabilities.

Model-conditional frequency

Produced by given rules and sampling design.

≠

Real-world occurrence frequency

Requires external materials and conditions for transfer.

Posterior probability

Updating from data under a prior and likelihood.

≠

Assumption-free objective truth

No formula automatically removes model conditions.

Qualitative direction

Also a conclusion requiring identification support.

≠

Default fallback answer

Evidence may permit opposing directions simultaneously.

Mathematical construction: one datum can yield a conditional posteriorTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEntirely a mathematical construction, with one success only inside the model; no actual trial or justification of a real-world prior.

Let unknown success rate θ∈[0,1] have an artificially stipulated uniform prior density 1, with conditionally independent identically distributed trials and one observed success, giving likelihood θ. The normalization constant ∫ from 0 to 1 θdθ=1/2, so posterior density is 2θ and next-trial posterior predictive mean is ∫ from 0 to 1 θ·2θdθ=2/3. This calculation depends on prior, observation, and generative assumptions, not ‘one observation reveals actual success rate 2/3’.

BoundaryDifferent priors, selective observation, or nonidentical distributions change the answer; neither small sample size nor the formula itself establishes real calibration.

Teaching construction: severity sets checking priority without assigning probabilityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsRisk types, windows, and resources are constructed; no actual emergency is described and no action authorized.

In a fictional system, path A may cause irreversible harm with a 10-minute response window, while B causes only reversible delay and can wait a day. Both probabilities are unknown, but explicit protective goals and current checking resources can prioritize A. Report ‘A checked first because of consequences and window; probability unknown’, not an invented ‘A has 80%’ to justify ranking.

BoundaryChecking itself still needs authority and safety boundaries; severe consequences are not an unconditional excuse to act.

Mathematical construction: oversampling frequency is not the original model probabilityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsProbabilities and quotas are stipulated, with no actual sampling; this shows only the distinction between design and target distributions.

A fictional model specifies P(A)=0.1 and P(non-A)=0.9. To examine A’s consequences, researchers deliberately generate 50 A and 50 non-A scenarios. The sample’s 50% A reflects a design quota, not a model probability changed to 0.5, much less a real probability. Estimating an expectation under the original model requires combining branch-conditional results with original weights 0.1 and 0.9.

BoundaryActual importance sampling also needs corresponding support and weight conditions; the example does not replace a full estimation procedure.

Simulated distributions in a 2020 paper: real-data input is not a real response processDocumented case

Perdomo and colleagues explicitly label §5.2 of their original paper as simulations: the base uses a subset of real credit data, but agent responses and distribution changes are model-stipulated. This section uses the published research design only to show that real data and simulated mechanisms may coexist, with the latter still retaining assumption status.

12.5Calibration and Evaluation ​

In briefEvaluation first asks what is evaluated, for which population, response regime, and horizon. A score answers a specified prediction question, not additionally how many outcomes action saved or who may act.

Foresight capability is established by results registered over time. It does not follow from a style that sounds accurate. Where applicable, evaluate probability tasks with the Brier score, log loss, calibration curves, resolution, and interval coverage. Use pre-registered ranking metrics for ranking tasks. Use precision, recall, or domain metrics for event detection. Use window coverage and lead time for predictions of timing.

Every metric must match the actual use. If low-probability events with severe harms call for caution, evaluation cannot rely only on overall accuracy. A false positive costs something different when the output prompts further observation than when it is used to compel action. Good metrics establish neither that the model’s explanation is correct nor that action is justified.

Once early warning is in use, the object of evaluation must specify the response regime. Is the task to predict actual events under an existing regime, or to ask separately what issuing a warning or taking action changed? Retain records of reach, execution, entries and exits of the objects, and how the data were produced, where these affect evaluation. When the regime changes, state again which outcomes are still comparable. The absence of an observed event cannot automatically be recorded as a false positive or taken to establish successful protection. A claim about harm avoided separately requires a causal comparison suited to that claim. Forecasts already defined under the current response regime can still be evaluated against the original target. There is no need to turn every prediction task into a study of intervention effects. The original target, horizon, and success rules must not be rewritten after the fact because a response took place (Perdomo et al., 2020). See also §2.4 and §12.6.

Evaluation DimensionQuestionAction After Failure
CalibrationOf events assigned 70%, do roughly 70% occur over the long run?Adjust the expression or downgrade probability outputs
ResolutionCan the model distinguish different risks or paths?Remove variables that make no contribution and return to the baseline
CoverageDo intervals or time windows cover the actual outcomes?Widen intervals or revise the clocks
Gain over baselineDoes it outperform the simple model?Stop making foresight claims for the complex model
StabilityDoes performance hold across times, locations, and boundaries?Restrict the domain of application or retire the model
Distribution of errorAt which positions do persistent underestimates or false positives occur?Review by people affected, remediation, and stronger protection

Three parallel questions can fix the terms of the evaluation.

QuestionWhat Sufficient Material Can AnswerWhat Must Be Retained
How did the original prediction perform on the frozen target?Compute loss, classification outcomes, or coverage using actual labels defined on the same basisA single case score does not establish long-run calibration. Do not enter zero for missing labels
How much did publication or action change the outcome?Give a limited effect estimate based on a causal comparison suited to the questionAn observed absence of the event cannot by itself distinguish initially low risk from successful prevention
Is it appropriate to adopt this prediction and response?Compare protection, false rejections, delay, distribution, and cost under explicit normative premisesNeither predictive accuracy nor a positive effect by itself confers permission

For example, suppose a forecast registered in advance assigns an event probability of 0.8 under the current response regime, and the complete label at the end of the horizon is 0. The Brier loss for that case is 0.64. If the threshold for binary classification was set in advance at 0.5, a false positive may also be recorded for that target. This limited calculation establishes neither the risk without action nor that the response was ineffective. If monitoring was offline and no label was obtained, the same calculation cannot be used. Complete labels for people who were approved or received services can directly evaluate only the corresponding population. Extending the evaluation to people who were rejected, were not reached, or exited requires labels for them or well-grounded methods of identification and bounding.

After a change in the response regime, first check whether the original target is still the same question. If the target is retained, report the performance change as observed. If the target shifts to a different response regime or population, create a new registration and retain the old results. Reflexivity must not be used to cancel a score that can be computed. One successful response must not be used to rescue all incorrect predictions after the fact.

12.5Note

Understanding this section

12.5 Calibration and Evaluation

Evaluation first asks what is evaluated, for which population, response regime, and horizon. A score answers a specified prediction question, not additionally how many outcomes action saved or who may act.

Foresight capability comes from preregistration, comparable outcomes, and continuing comparison, not fluent retrospective explanation. Freeze original targets, horizons, success rules, and information cutoffs. A single case can be scored but cannot certify long-term calibration. Outcome-material formation, missingness, and entry/exit also form evaluation conditions.

Measures depend on the task: probability forecasts may use Brier scores, log loss, calibration curves, and resolution; prediction intervals also need coverage and width. Rankings use predetermined ranking measures, event detection precision/recall or proportionate domain measures, and timing predictions window coverage and lead time. An attractive number cannot replace the originally relevant target.

This guide uses the binary single-event Brier convention L=(p−y)², lower being better; log loss uses natural logarithms, L=−[y ln p+(1−y)ln(1−p)], with infinite loss for probabilities 0 or 1 facing opposite labels. The original multiclass-vector form may differ by a constant factor from this convention; align definitions across reports first. Unsupported probabilities should not be invented just to use a measure.

Calibration asks whether long-run probabilities correspond to observed proportions among comparable forecasts; resolution asks whether objects of differing risk can be distinguished. Reporting one population rate for everyone may be overall calibrated yet have no discriminatory resolution. Chance bin agreement in finite samples does not establish future calibration; sample size, uncertainty, binning, and applicability also matter.

Each of the original’s six evaluation dimensions has a corrective direction. Failed calibration may change expression or downgrade probabilities; weak resolution may remove unhelpful variables or return to baseline; poor coverage may revise intervals or mechanism clocks; no baseline gain stops the complex model’s gain claim; instability across times/locations narrows the domain or retires the model; recurrent underestimation or false alarms at specific positions require affected-party review, remedies, and stronger protection. Wider intervals may improve coverage while losing usefulness; do not optimize one number alone.

Use determines error costs and required reports. Observation reminders and coercive measures may share a score but impose different false-alarm burdens; low-probability high-harm tasks cannot report overall accuracy alone. Show errors by burden-bearing position, population, and phase so averages do not hide sustained false denials, delays, or misses. Excellent measures prove neither correct mechanisms nor normative legitimacy.

Published forecasts may affect action, which may alter actual events; specify the response regime. Preserve reach, actual execution, entry/exit, data formation, and institutional-change records. For targets defined as actual events under the current response regime, score actual labels normally. ‘The model affected reality’ cannot cancel a valid score, nor must every prediction evaluation be converted into intervention-effect research.

Three parallel questions do not replace one another: prediction performance for a frozen target, using comparable labels for loss/classification/coverage; how publication or action changed outcomes, requiring proportionate causal comparison; and appropriateness of prediction/response, requiring explicit norms, protection, costs, distribution, and authority. ‘No event observed’ alone proves neither false alarm nor successful protection; return to target, label, and response definitions.

Specifically, if the preregistered target is the actual event under the current response regime, p=0.8 with complete endpoint label y=0 gives Brier=0.64; with a prior threshold 0.5, this target’s false positive may also be recorded. The calculation says nothing about what would happen without action. If monitoring is offline and y unknown, do not substitute 0. Complete labels only for service recipients directly support only that group, not labels for unreached, rejected, or exited people.

After institutional change, first ask whether the question remains the same. With unchanged targets, report performance changes and comparability limits honestly; a target under a different regime or population needs new registration, preserving old predictions and scores. Do not post hoc change ‘will occur under the current regime’ to ‘would occur without response’ to rescue an erroneous prediction.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Freeze target, population, horizon, information cutoff, scoring convention, and response regime.

  2. 2

    Choose measures for actual use and clearly record comparable labels, missingness, and formation processes.

  3. 3

    Compute valid scores for the original forecasts; missing labels are not nonoccurrence.

  4. 4

    Identify publication/action causal effects separately; no event alone cannot prove successful prevention.

  5. 5

    Separately compare adoption options through norms, protection, distribution, and authority; scores cannot sign authorization.

  6. 6

    Adjust domain and output strength through the six-dimensional evaluation; changed targets require new registration while preserving old outcomes.

Distinctions to keep clear

Single-case loss

Calculated for one frozen prediction and complete label.

≠

Long-term calibration

Whether long-run probabilities and occurrence proportions match for comparable predictions.

Calibration

Correspondence between probabilities and frequencies.

≠

Resolution

Ability to distinguish objects of differing risk.

Prediction evaluation

Performance for a target under the current response regime.

≠

Intervention effect

How much actual response changes outcomes relative to suitable comparison conditions.

Complete zero label

The event is confirmed absent under its definition.

≠

Label unavailable

Monitoring may be offline or selectively invisible; zero cannot fill it.

Excellent within-domain performance

Performance for specified population, target, and regime.

≠

Generalizable and justified

Still needs transfer, distributional, normative, and authority arguments.

Mathematical construction: why Brier prefers true probability within a fixed generative modelTeaching scenario

AssumptionsOne fixed target and distribution, p,q∈[0,1]; mathematics only, no actual trial.

Let Y be Bernoulli with parameter q and prediction p. Expected loss q(1−p)²+(1−q)p²=p²−2pq+q=(p−q)²+q(1−q). The second term is independent of p; the first is nonnegative and zero only at p=q, so expectation is minimized at p=q. This algebraic proof within a specified generative model does not infer true model parameters backward from one low score.

BoundaryRegime changes, selective labels, or mismatched targets prevent direct reuse of one q; this property certifies neither causal explanations nor action authority.

Mathematical construction: bin calibration can match while resolution differsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsLabels, groups, and probabilities are stipulated; no actual fitting, calibration sample, or independent test.

Construct 20 complete labels: 2 of 10 low-risk items and 8 of 10 high-risk items are 1. The model predicts 0.2 and 0.8 respectively. Each group’s Brier sum is 2×0.8²+8×0.2²=1.6, giving overall mean 3.2/20=0.16. A baseline predicts 0.5 for all; 10 of 20 events match 0.5 overall, but each loss is 0.25 and risks are not distinguished. This finite construction only illustrates bin frequencies versus resolution.

BoundaryExact matching over 20 items is not long-term calibration; groups must be predetermined and evaluation labels must not select models retrospectively.

Teaching construction: 0.64 is calculable, how much was prevented is notTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPure teaching construction; potential outcomes illustrate identification boundaries, with no actual action or randomized trial.

A fictional warning contract explicitly predicts events under the current response regime, registering p=0.8, threshold 0.5, and complete endpoint label y=0. Brier=(0.8−0)²=0.64 and log loss −ln0.2≈1.609; predicted positive and actually negative permits this target’s false positive. If action occurred and observed Y(action)=0, Y(no action) may be 0 or 1: the former means occurrence was unchanged, the latter one event prevented. The current observation cannot distinguish these two constructed worlds.

BoundaryIf monitoring was offline and y unavailable, this calculation fails; if the original target was not an event under current response, evaluate under its original contract rather than changing labels to fit the formula.

Perdomo et al.’s 2020 paper opens by discussing how predictions used for decisions may change predicted outcomes and formalizes this through a model-parameter-dependent distribution D(θ). This is published theoretical modeling offering methodological guidance on explicit response regimes, not proof that a particular warning saved outcomes.

Why does p=0.8,y=0 give loss 0.64 rather than 0.2?

This guide’s binary Brier squares probability error: (0.8−0)²=0.64; 0.2 is the predicted probability of nonoccurrence.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Which two causal situations are both compatible with no event?

Either the event would not have occurred anyway, or it would have occurred but response prevented it. A zero after action alone cannot distinguish them.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

If a model reports 0.5 for everyone and half have events, does it have good resolution?

No. One probability for everyone may match overall while failing to distinguish the constructed 0.2 and 0.8 groups.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Must old scores be discarded when the response regime changes?

No. With the same target, report changed performance and comparison limits; changed targets require new registration, preserving old results.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

May missing labels be conservatively recorded as zero?

No. Zero confirms nonoccurrence; unknown remains unknown, with coverage and missingness mechanisms separately recorded.
