12.6Early Signals, Contrary Signals, and Trigger Points ​

In briefUseful lead time runs through completion of protection, not merely appearance of an alarm on a screen. Signals trigger review; they cannot replace path explanation, normative judgment, or authority to act.

An early signal is an observable change that the path’s mechanism should produce first. A smaller version of the outcome does not suffice. A contrary signal indicates that a key condition of the path is failing or that a competing path is gaining support. Both must be registered before results to avoid collecting only supporting material.

Trigger points connect foresight to review. Observing a signal calls for reassessing the object, path, probability, normative grounds, and authorization. It does not automatically trigger action. High-risk cases should also have veto triggers, such as a breach of the protection floor, inability of key affected people to exit, distortion of data sources, or deteriorating model calibration.

Use completion of a feasible action as the endpoint when comparing clocks. Detecting the signal, verifying it, publishing the warning, reaching people, and understanding the warning each involve a delay. Gathering resources takes time, as can carrying out a transfer or waiting for a measure to take effect. Earlier algorithmic detection does not guarantee that the last person affected can receive protection before harm occurs. If no harm follows an alert, use the frozen target and labeling conditions to decide whether an operational false positive may be registered. Identify separately whether a successful response prevented harm. Keep the denominators separate for the operational false positive rate, the proportion of false alerts among alerts, and the missed detection rate. 〔Studies 31.05〕

12.6Note

Understanding this section

12.6 Early signals, contrary signals, and trigger points

Useful lead time runs through completion of protection, not merely appearance of an alarm on a screen. Signals trigger review; they cannot replace path explanation, normative judgment, or authority to act.

Early signals should precede outcomes through the discussed path's mechanism and have observable definitions. For a backlog path, an early change might be arrivals persistently exceeding processing, not a smaller number restating the final backlog in advance. Register observation position, definition, window, and relationship to the path. Without those bridges, any preceding phenomenon could retrospectively be packaged as a precursor.

Contrary signals concern failure of key conditions or support for competing paths. They need not prove the final outcome impossible; they weaken the current path's grounds. Register both signal types before outcomes, specifying which records count as observation and which reflect missing monitoring. Searching only for support removes foresight's possibility of failure.

Trigger points connect observation to review of object identity, path conditions, probability expression, norms, and authorization. A detected signal does not automatically permit action. If an explicitly lawful preauthorization procedure exists, act within its conditions and limits; this section's abstract rule cannot create authority by itself.

High-risk veto triggers should be explicit beforehand: a breached protection floor, key affected people unable to exit, distorted data sources, deteriorating calibration, and so forth. Applicable rules require suspension or veto of the corresponding option and protection review, not merely a slight confidence reduction while continuing unchanged. They also need not stop every task unrelated to the defect.

The clock ends at completed action or effective protection. Detection, verification, issuance, reach, understanding, funding or allocation, transfer, and onset may each take time, differently across positions. Average reach cannot establish completion for the last or hardest-to-reach person. Parallel stages need dependency-based critical-path calculations; only serial delays add directly. Retain unknown delays as unknowns or grounded intervals.

Algorithmic lead time is hazard time minus detection time. Actual protection margin also subtracts time needed for downstream completion. Technical advance notice does not mean every affected person has enough time; communication, understanding, resources, and actual capability can bottleneck. Addressing bottlenecks requires more than greater predictive precision: examine endpoint conditions and protective responsibilities.

No harm after an alarm still returns to frozen targets and labels. If the target is the actual event under the current response regime, with complete labels and predetermined thresholds, an operational false positive may be registered. Whether response prevented harm needs a separate causal comparison. Unreached people and missing records cannot default to safety, and “successful protection” cannot retrospectively rescue every warning.

Three easily confused rates require numerators, denominators, population, and window. Under a fixed binary classification, operational false-positive rate FPR=FP/(FP+TN), false-alarm fraction among alerts FAR=FP/(TP+FP), and false-negative rate FNR=FN/(TP+FN). Names vary across domains; formulas matter more than abbreviations. A zero denominator makes the rate undefined, not zero. Precision TP/(TP+FP) and recall TP/(TP+FN) may be reported separately and must not be interchanged.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First explain why the path generates the preceding change, registering observable signals and contrary evidence.

  2. 2

    Fix thresholds, windows, missing-data handling, and veto triggers before outcomes.

  3. 3

    Observation triggers review, not automatic action. Check object, path, expression, norms, and authority individually.

  4. 4

    End the clock at completable protection; check critical paths and resources for every bearing position.

  5. 5

    Compute operational metrics under frozen targets and report denominators separately. Identify prevented-harm effects independently.

Distinctions to keep clear

Early signal

An observable change expected earlier by the mechanism.

≠

A smaller version of the outcome

Describing the outcome early without a mechanism bridge.

Contrary signal

Weakens a key path condition or supports a competing explanation.

≠

Absolute exclusion of the outcome

Needs stronger evidence and does not follow automatically.

Algorithmic lead time

Hazard time minus detection time.

≠

Protection margin

Also subtracts reach, understanding, resources, and action-onset delays.

False-positive rate

False positives among all actual negatives.

≠

False-alarm fraction among alerts

False positives among all alarms.

Triggered review

Checks whether conditions and responsibilities still hold.

≠

Automatic authorization

Cannot arise from observing a signal itself.

Teaching construction: early and contrary signals must connect to mechanismsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsQueue, values, and criteria are teaching constructions, with no actual system experiment.

A fictional queue starts with backlog 6. Over the next two hours, arrivals are 2/hour and processing 1/hour, giving backlogs 7 then 8. Preregister an early signal of complete first-hour records showing 2 arrivals and 1 completion, and a contrary signal of second-hour evidence that capacity rose to 3 and 3 were actually processed. If the latter occurs, the endpoint is 6 rather than the original path's 8. Seeing only “capacity-expansion application submitted” does not establish increased actual processing.

BoundaryUnrecorded arrivals or false completion records invalidate signal status and require source checks. The contrary signal revises the current path, not proves backlog impossible forever.

Mathematical construction: a 30-minute warning can still be lateTeaching scenario

AssumptionsEvery time and serial dependency is artificial; no actual drill or disaster response occurred.

Let hazard time be minute 30 and signal detection minute 0. Fully serial verification 3, issuance 2, reach 8, understanding 4, resource allocation 6, and action onset 10 total 33 minutes, leaving protection margin 30−33=−3. Another object requires only 2 minutes for reach, totaling 27 with margin 3. Both have the same 30-minute algorithmic lead, yet timely protection cannot be claimed for both. Reducing the first object's reach to 4 gives total 29 and margin 1. This is only clock arithmetic under stated conditions.

BoundaryActual stages may overlap, delays have distributions, and hazard times have error. Check critical paths and uncertainty. This calculation is not emergency-operating advice.

Mathematical construction: the same 18 false positives, three different denominatorsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThreshold, target, response regime, population, and horizon are fixed. All 100 labels are constructed.

Construct 100 consistently defined, fully labeled objects: TP=8, FP=18, FN=2, TN=72. Operational false-positive rate is 18/(18+72)=20%; false-alarm fraction among alerts is 18/(8+18)=9/13≈69.23%; false-negative rate is 2/(8+2)=20%. Precision is 8/26≈30.77%, recall 8/10=80%. The two 20% values coincide only in this example; the metrics are not identical.

BoundaryIf labels cover only response recipients, this complete-population confusion matrix cannot be reused directly. Classification does not identify the number saved by intervention.

Actual institutional design: WMO lists dissemination and response capability separatelyDocumented case

WMO's 2023 overview of the Early Warnings for All action plan lists four pillars: risk knowledge, monitoring and forecasting, warning dissemination and communication, and preparedness and response capability. This public design retains dissemination and response as separate areas of development, reminding readers that completed detection is not completed end-to-end protection.

12.7Failure Semantics for Forecasts ​

In briefForecast honesty lies not only in cautious publication but in allowing the original record to be judged unsupported, unresolved, or unevaluable at expiry. Giving failure a vague new name does not improve accuracy.

When the horizon ends, the result can be supported, unsupported, unresolved, target invalid, or not evaluable. Unresolved is the state of insufficient evidence specified by the contract. It is no compromise between success and failure. A result that cannot be evaluated must state what went wrong with the data, object, horizon, or execution. An invalid target means the object of the prediction or its identity criterion has undergone conversion. It must not be counted as a hit.

Changing the target, horizon, or scope of circles after results, or merging several paths into “it happened to some extent,” cannot preserve the original forecast’s eligibility to count as a success. A new interpretation can be recorded in a new version. The old record remains.

12.7Note

Understanding this section

12.7 Failure semantics for foresight

Forecast honesty lies not only in cautious publication but in allowing the original record to be judged unsupported, unresolved, or unevaluable at expiry. Giving failure a vague new name does not improve accuracy.

This section gives five meanings for evaluation at expiry: supported, unsupported, unresolved, target invalidated, and cannot evaluate. Return to the prior contract's target, identity criterion, window, material, and success rules rather than selecting face-saving labels. Rules must also specify overlap handling beforehand; the five names are not an automatic classifier needing no explanation.

Supported means obtained material meets the original contract's support rule, only within the original scope, not proof of every mechanism, probability, or extension. Unsupported means the original support criterion did not hold; complete observations contradicting the original assertion may be explicitly reported as failure. One occurrence or nonoccurrence does not automatically validate or invalidate a probability. Use the original scoring and long-term evaluation.

Unresolved is a defined, contract-permitted state of insufficient evidence. For example, a measurement-error interval crosses the predetermined threshold, so the available complete material cannot distinguish the sides. It is not half a success or permission to extend deadlines indefinitely until favorable material arrives. Any allowed supplementary observation procedure must be registered beforehand, retaining the original expiry status.

Cannot evaluate must identify the failed prerequisite, such as permanently lost key data, an untraceable object, an inoperable horizon definition, or unclear execution records. The contract should distinguish it from unresolved: the former may mean the evaluation procedure's entry conditions are unusable, the latter that entry remains usable but evidence cannot decide. This operational distinction is this lesson's contract illustration, not an assertion that the original supplies one exhaustive, unique algorithm.

Target invalidated means the original forecast object or identity criterion actually converted. If a specified service unit is abolished and its tasks and members absorbed elsewhere, and the original contract specifies no uptake relation, the new organization's outcomes cannot masquerade as a hit for the old object. Object change needs material; unfavorable results cannot declare identity change.

Changing targets, horizons, or circle scope after outcomes, or merging competing paths into “something happened a little,” cannot retain the original foresight's success eligibility. Acknowledge the original result and create a version for a new question, object, or conditions. Old registration, evidence, and scores remain, with traceable revision reasons.

Failure semantics is a correction interface, not evasive language. Unresolved specifies missing distinguishing material; cannot evaluate explains why evaluation cannot run; target invalidated demonstrates identity conversion and states continuing monitoring and remedial responsibilities. Excluding difficult objects en masse cannot improve claimed hit rates. Summaries should show counts for all statuses, total original registrations, and the evaluable subset, avoiding selective denominators.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Check target, object identity, window, material, and decision criteria under the original contract.

  2. 2

    If material meets support rules, mark support within scope. Record complete contrary outcomes honestly as unsupported.

  3. 3

    Mark insufficient evidence unresolved under predetermined rules; explain cannot evaluate when procedural entry is broken.

  4. 4

    If identity converted without contractual uptake, record target invalidated rather than a false hit.

  5. 5

    Give new explanations separate versions, retain old records, and disclose all statuses and denominators in summaries.

Distinctions to keep clear

Unresolved

Contract-defined evidence insufficiency; the answer remains unknown.

≠

Half a success

Converting unknowns into hits without a definition distorts results.

Cannot evaluate

Required procedural, material, or object conditions cannot be met.

≠

Forecast confirmed

Insufficient material cannot become positive evidence.

Target invalidated

Material supports conversion of object or identity criterion.

≠

Changing objects afterward

Moving forecast scope to preserve success.

New-version explanation

Separately establishes targets and conditions while retaining old results.

≠

Rewriting old success

Backfilling new conditions into an expired old record.

One event outcome

Supports a specific classification or case-specific loss.

≠

Long-term probability correctness

Requires corresponding comparable registrations and calibration evaluation.

Teaching construction: five expiry records under one threshold contractTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll objects, numbers, contract rules, and events are teaching constructions; the original prediction is a threshold assertion, not a probability statement.

Fictional registration: backlog B≥8 in specified unit A at the end of hour 2. The contract permits direct judgment from exact records with matching definitions; a valid error interval crossing 8 is unresolved; unrecoverable loss of core count data makes evaluation impossible; abolition of A without a succession definition invalidates the target. Five independent hypothetical cases are: complete B=9, supported; complete B=6, not supported; valid interval [7,9], unresolved; destroyed logs with no reconstruction, unable to evaluate; unit A abolished and merged without continuity of the original identity, target invalid. These are alternative cases, not five simultaneous outcomes in one run.

BoundaryActual contracts may use other explicit criteria; identity succession and credible error intervals require separate material.

Teaching construction: changing the deadline creates a new result, not rescue of an old predictionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsTimes and values are constructed, with no actual queue observations.

The original registered prediction is B≥8 at t=2. Complete observation B2=6 leaves it unsupported. Later B3=9 at t=3 does not let the author change the t=2 record to success by saying “it will eventually reach 8.” New information may support a new registration for t=3 or later, but its registration time must be explicit; after knowing B3=9, it cannot be presented as a prior prediction.

BoundaryIf the original contract had predicted a 2-to-3-hour window, evaluate under that original window. Here the original target is explicitly t=2 only.

Mathematical construction: disclose status distributions instead of counting unknowns as half-successTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe ten statuses are mathematical constructions, and the binary-evaluable set is explicitly defined in the assumptions.

Suppose 10 registrations resolve: 4 supported, 2 not supported, 2 unresolved, 1 target invalid, and 1 unable to evaluate. Under this construction's prespecified rules, support among the 6 binary-evaluable items is 4/6≈66.67%; supported items among all registrations are 4/10=40%. These answer different questions and both require denominators plus the other four statuses. The two unresolved items cannot each count as half a success to yield 5/10=50% labeled a hit rate, nor may the other four be hidden.

BoundaryThe evaluable support proportion is not overall calibration, causal correctness, or real-world generalizability; unlike tasks cannot be pooled without weighting and separated definitions.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleAn unresolved result at resolution is scored half success and half failure.

What it limitsUnresolved is an evidence status. Unless the original task has an independently justified, preregistered scoring rule, it cannot arbitrarily be converted into hits.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThe original unit was abolished and a new team met the target, so the old prediction hit.

What it limitsFirst check identity-succession rules; without them, the target is invalid rather than an old success.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleA hit in hour three proves the hour-two assertion correct.

What it limitsTime belongs to the frozen target; deadlines cannot be changed afterward.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The five statuses are not arbitrary defensive words; judgment grounds must be reviewable.
  • This lesson illustrates the contract boundary between unresolved and cannot evaluate without turning it into the theory's sole necessary definition.
  • Object-identity conversion and data loss both need factual support; failure itself cannot establish either.
  • Reporting accuracy only among evaluable cases while hiding other statuses misleads about the full registration set.

Scope and open questions

This section concerns the original evaluation contract and status semantics. Individually checkable teaching constructions isolate logical boundaries; historical events lacking complete prior contracts are not forcibly classified.

  • Actual projects require frozen contracts, identity-succession rules, and resolution material before the five statuses can be judged; no actual project is currently being empirically classified.

Check your understanding

  1. 1

    Why does B's valid interval [7,9] remain unresolved under this contract?

  2. 2

    Why is destruction of logs not automatically unsupported?

  3. 3

    May both 4/6 and 4/10 be reported for the ten items?

  4. 4

    Are new explanations prohibited?

Why does B's valid interval [7,9] remain unresolved under this contract?

Threshold 8 lies within the interval, so attainment and nonattainment remain possible. The input material is valid but insufficient to distinguish them.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why is destruction of logs not automatically unsupported?

Under this demonstration contract, labels cannot be recovered and evaluation cannot run; absent evidence cannot be entered as a complete contrary result.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

May both 4/6 and 4/10 be reported for the ten items?

Yes, naming them respectively the support rate in the binary-evaluable subset and the supported proportion of all registrations, while disclosing other statuses.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Are new explanations prohibited?

A new version is allowed, but registration time, target, grounds, and the old failure must remain; original success eligibility cannot be rewritten.

12.8The Bridge From Foresight to Bounded Choice ​

In brief“This may be better” can become advice for deliberation, but not directly a binding command to others. Conditional consequences, value comparisons, and actual permissions each need their own reasons.
Codes used in this section (1)
  • C12Check on the Validity of Normative Bridging

Foresight outputs answer only questions about conditional consequences. An analytical recommendation requires explicit normative premises, evidence, affected positions, options, costs and benefits, and conditions for revising the judgment. A recommendation does not confer permission to execute. Before real-world adoption, the record must also include explicit normative premises, the choosing subject, jurisdiction, affected positions, rights floors, options, the distribution of costs and benefits, authorization, stopping, appeal, rollback, and remedy. N, PF, J, O, and C12 still apply. Prediction provides no shortcut.

Prediction cannot automatically confer authorization. Even an extremely probable path does not show that anyone has authority to compel others to bear the cost of avoiding it. Even the highest average benefit does not show that the rights of positions in the minority may be ignored. Even if the model recommends taking no action, continuing harm and responsibility arising from inaction still require review.

12.8Note

Understanding this section

12.8 The Bridge from Foresight to Bounded Choice

“This may be better” can become advice for deliberation, but not directly a binding command to others. Conditional consequences, value comparisons, and actual permissions each need their own reasons.

Foresight states what may happen under conditions; it does not itself decide which consequences deserve pursuit or who should bear costs. High probability strengthens judgment about a consequence without alone expanding authority over others. High average benefits also cannot cancel rights at minority positions.

Before forming an analytical recommendation, make normative premises, evidence status, affected positions, candidate options, costs and benefits, and revision conditions explicit. Reasoned local judgments and conditional advice are possible without banning all analysis because execution is not yet authorized. Clearly mark their deliberative status and unmet conditions for actual adoption.

Before actual adoption, supply the choosing subject and jurisdiction, affected and low-power positions, rights floors, options and cost-benefit distributions, authorization, stopping, appeal, rollback, and remedies. This invokes existing N, PF, J, O, and C12, not a new shortcut from “accurate prediction” to execution.

Under §14.3 (Chinese source lines 2950–2968), N must be explicitly registered at runtime. N1 only prevents explanation from directly authorizing action and supplies no positive objective alone; N2 requires protection not be downgraded; N3 requires corrigibility of high-impact judgments; N4 opposes unlimited, inescapable unilateral sacrifice; N5 prevents treating persistence and selection as justification. Disclose selected principles, whether they are objectives or constraints, and how conflicts are handled rather than silently relying on a benevolent slogan.

PF is a protection floor that cannot freely be traded for efficiency. Section 14.8 (Chinese source lines 3038–3070) requires ten items to connect individually to actual mechanisms, responsibilities, stopping, appeals, review, rollback, and expiry; formal checkmarks are insufficient. Human, sentient, mixed, or unknown objects cannot be declared purely technical to reduce protection. Nor does the floor exhaust substantive rights; specific rights still require independent grounds.

J answers who has valid grounds to perform which action on which object, within what territory and period. Section 14.6 (Chinese source lines 3010–3023) requires one valid atomic tuple to cover an action's full scope. Permission to “read A” and “modify B” cannot combine into “modify A.” Lawful continuation across multiple actors may hold, but each action requires checking its own permissions and input conditions.

O1 freezes description, evidence, and uncertainty; O2 explicitly lists norms, burden bearers, and conflicts; O3 compares options including inaction and checks authorization boundaries; O4 implements bounded execution with monitoring, stopping, appeal, rollback, remedies, and expiry. Under §4.14.1 (Chinese source lines 932–949), C12 checks completeness of bridging components; it neither chooses values for people nor replaces actual institutions' legal validity.

Inaction also requires evaluating consequences and responsibilities: old rules may keep causing harm, waiting may miss a protective window, and existing duties do not disappear because a model recommends no new action. Specify responsibilities for observation, protection, and reopening assessment rather than automatically presenting inaction as neutral, costless, and needing no explanation.

Localize gaps: insufficient evidence blocks corresponding judgments, unclear norms block recommendations depending on them, and insufficient authorization blocks corresponding execution. Independently established descriptions, conditional advice with explicit premises, and evidence needs may remain. Neither execute beyond authority nor refuse all grounded help because one gate fails.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Separate conditional consequences from worthwhile objectives, listing evidence and uncertainty.

  2. 2

    Specify positive norms and protective constraints, comparing costs and benefits of candidates and inaction position by position.

  3. 3

    Form a bounded recommendation for deliberation with revision conditions, preserving its lack of required permissions.

  4. 4

    Before actual adoption, check the subject, J, PF, and O1–O4, then use C12 to check bridging completeness.

  5. 5

    Execution must allow stopping, appeal, rollback, remedies, and expiry; inaction also records continuing responsibilities.

Distinctions to keep clear

Analytical recommendation

A grounded local or conditional recommendation under explicit premises.

≠

Actual adoption

Also requires complete protection, permissions, procedures, and correction conditions.

High probability

Strengthens descriptive judgment about the consequence in question.

≠

Power to compel others

Requires independent valid authorization and justification.

Average benefit

An aggregate indicator of some benefit or cost.

≠

Distribution and rights

Who bears burdens, whether refusal is possible, and which floors are not exchangeable.

C12 check

Whether normative-bridging components are complete.

≠

Sources of values and actual authorization

Cannot be created by the checklist itself.

No additional action

The proposed new action is not implemented.

≠

No continuing responsibility

Existing duties, harms, and protective needs may remain.

Mathematical construction: average benefits can hide concentrated harmTeaching scenario

AssumptionsUtilities, population, and rights constraints are stipulated; no actual harm measurement or proof of interpersonal utility comparability is supplied.

Fictional option A gives utility +2 to each of 9 positions and −30 to 1 low-power position: total 18−30=−12, mean −1.2. Option B gives +5 to each of 9 and −30 to the last: total 45−30=15, mean +1.5. Even with positive mean B, if −30 represents a rights harm the assumptions prohibit shifting, average benefits alone cannot justify adoption. Numerical utilities illustrate aggregation's concealment; the rights constraint is not derived from numerical magnitude.

BoundaryWithout comparable utilities, even summation cannot serve as an actual comparison. Rights constraints must be independently explicit, not added afterward because the author dislikes a result.

Teaching construction: recommending deliberation is not changing schedulesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe team, objectives, and prediction are teaching constructions, with no actual personnel or organizational operation.

A fictional team forecasts reduced waiting under voluntary rotation. The analyst explicitly aims to reduce waiting without weakening existing rest protections, compares current arrangements, reinforcements, and voluntary rotation, and identifies who bears extra burdens and what evidence would change the judgment. The analyst may therefore recommend submitting voluntary rotation for deliberation. Without scheduling authority and implemented consent, appeal, and rollback mechanisms, they cannot directly alter actual schedules.

BoundaryVoluntariness is not treated as established. Actual consent must permit refusal and withdrawal and comply with applicable institutions; no legal judgment on particular labor rules is provided.

Formal construction: permissions cannot be combined across objectsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll subjects, objects, and authorizations are formal constructions; record contents are assumed valid but limited as stated.

Suppose J1 permits subject A only to read object A this week, and J2 permits that subject only to modify object B this week. The candidate action is modifying A this week. J1 mismatches the action and J2 the object, so neither fully covers it. Taking the Cartesian product of their object and action columns manufactures nonexistent permission.

BoundaryThis does not deny lawful workflows where multiple subjects perform different actions; each action still needs complete coverage of its own.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexamplePrediction confidence is 99%, so anyone may be forced to bear preventive costs.

What it limitsConfidence concerns conditional consequences; cost distribution, rights, and jurisdiction require separate examination.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleExecution permission has not been supplied, so even conditional recommendations cannot be written.

What it limitsEvidence-based deliberative recommendations with explicit norms may be written, without presenting them as authorized execution.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThe model recommends inaction, so protection and observation responsibilities end.

What it limitsInaction retains ongoing consequences and existing duties; evaluate them and arrange reopening conditions.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Lack of authorization does not prohibit analytical recommendations for deliberation, but must prevent their treatment as executable commands.
  • Positive aggregate net benefit cannot alone override harm to rights at low-power positions.
  • Several incomplete authorization fragments for an action cannot be assembled into complete valid permission.
  • N1 is a negative gate, insufficient to choose a positive proposal by itself.

Scope and open questions

This section concerns normative bridging and permission logic; explicit fictional comparisons and formal tuples suffice to illustrate boundaries. No actual decision file verifies all authorization, protection, and correction conditions, so historical success or failure is not forced into normative certification.

  • Actual choices still need the present norms, affected-person material, valid authorization, and evidence of accessible correction; this lesson grants no eligibility for actual adoption.

  3. 3

No. First register explicit norms and conflicts; C12 checks corresponding bridges rather than secretly creating objectives.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why may option B with average +1.5 still be rejected?

The stipulated rights constraint prohibits shifting that harm onto the last position; the mean cannot cancel an independent constraint.

No. One lacks action coverage and the other object coverage; they cannot combine into new permission.

12.9The Option Set Must Include Action and No Action ​

In briefComparing options is not finding reasons for a predetermined action. First lay out genuinely available paths worth comparing, especially retaining the no-additional-action baseline and distinguishing active maintenance of current arrangements from doing nothing.

When generating options, check the applicability of each of six categories: maintaining the status quo, acting proactively, delaying action, taking a small exploratory action, exiting or transferring, and explicitly taking no action. For each applicable category, develop genuine and comparable options. Explain why any category does not apply. Do not invent options to meet a quota. If a choice is requested, do not remove the explicit no-action baseline or combine it with maintaining the status quo. Maintaining the status quo may require ongoing resources and execution. Taking no action may allow existing conditions to change on their own. Specific tasks may add options. Tasks that do not request a choice need not produce a list of actions.

Option TypeMain UseRisks That Must Be Checked
Maintain the status quoProtect existing stability and uptake arrangementsHidden costs, continuing harm, and lock-in
Proactive actionChange a path or its conditions quicklyAuthority, irreversibility, and cross-circle spillovers
Delayed actionWait for information, procedure, or the right timeHarm and lost opportunities from delay itself
Exploratory actionObtain information through a small reversible stepWho bears the costs of the trial and whether it can actually be rolled back
Exit or transferEnd an unsuitable object or relationshipPeople unable to exit, responsibilities, and preservation of history
No actionAvoid overstepping authority or taking high-risk actionBias toward the default, continuing consequences, and responsibility for inaction

Taking no action does not mean that nothing happens. Other actors, circles, resources, and clocks are still changing. The no-action option must have a baseline time, expected path, observation plan, conditions for reopening the decision, and a responsible party.

12.9Note

Understanding this section

12.9 The Option Set Must Include Action and Inaction

Comparing options is not finding reasons for a predetermined action. First lay out genuinely available paths worth comparing, especially retaining the no-additional-action baseline and distinguishing active maintenance of current arrangements from doing nothing.

When the user or task requests a choice, examine six types individually: maintain the status quo, act proactively, delay action, take a small exploratory step, exit or transfer, and explicitly do not act. This checks applicability, not mandatory completion of six buttons. Explain constraints where inapplicable; construct actual comparable options where applicable. Tasks may add options, while pure explanation or verification tasks need no compulsory action list.

Maintaining the status quo may require continuing resources, rules, protections, and costs. Inaction means not implementing this proposed additional action, while existing mechanisms continue changing. Under §14.4 (Chinese source lines 2970–2993), the inaction baseline retains existing maintenance, ongoing conduct, and independent obligations; “no addition” cannot be replaced with “turn off all existing protection.” Specify each difference between active maintenance and baseline rather than merely renaming.

Maintaining the status quo requires checking hidden costs, ongoing harm, and lock-in; active intervention requires checking permissions, irreversibility, and costs spilling across circles. Rapid change is not necessarily worth pursuing, and stability is not necessarily justified. Both directions must disclose normative premises and affected positions.

Delayed action is an option with a clock: specify what material or procedure is awaited, for how long, who observes, and when review reopens. Waiting itself can accumulate harm or miss an opportunity window. Missing evidence cannot justify indefinite delay without responsibility, nor can planned future execution be registered as already having occurred.

A tentative small step must specify what is to be learned, distinguishing signals, scale, deadline, stopping, rollback, and who bears costs. Small scale means only that some quantity is small; it does not guarantee low risk or reversibility. Affected parties, privacy, irreversible information disclosure, and shifted burdens still require checks. Section 12.11 develops the detailed conditions.

Exit or transfer may end an unsuitable relationship or object, but does not automatically erase dependents, existing responsibilities, or history. Check who can exit, who cannot, who takes up the service or responsibility, and how records are preserved. Without qualified uptake, do not invent “just transfer it” to fill an option slot. Nor may exit be held hostage by unlimited responsibility.

Inaction must record the baseline time, expected path, observation plan, reopening conditions, and responsible party. Other actors, resources, and clocks continue moving; the baseline is not a still photograph. Only with this baseline can one compare what additional interference brings; otherwise “we must do something” readily becomes a hidden premise.

The six categories are not naturally mutually exclusive categories of the world. A combined option may begin with monitoring, proceed to a bounded trial, and transfer once a threshold is reached. Registration must distinguish stages, triggers, and resources, without counting the same action's benefits under multiple options or hiding execution-permission gaps behind a combined label. Real-world adoption still requires the bridging in 12.8; an option list does not itself authorize action.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Confirm whether the task requests choice; if so, check the applicability of all six categories.

  2. 2

    Specify which ongoing obligations and maintenance the inaction baseline retains, distinguishing them from additional active maintenance.

  3. 3

    For applicable options, record actual actions, objects, timing, resources, bearers, and boundaries.

  4. 4

    Explain the respective risks of delay, trials, and exit; do not rely on labels to guarantee safety or feasibility.

  5. 5

    Compare against the changing baseline in the same window; specify observation, reopening conditions, and responsibility, with permissions for adoption checked separately.

Distinctions to keep clear

Actively maintaining the status quo

Requires explicit resources and execution to preserve the target state.

≠

No additional action

Preserves existing processes, while the state may still change naturally.

Applicability checks for six categories

Explain why each category applies or does not apply.

≠

Six options that must exist

Would force the invention of options lacking resources or permissions.

Time-limited delay

Waits for specified information and bears the price of waiting.

≠

Indefinite procrastination

Sets no observation, deadline, or responsibility for reopening.

Exit or transfer

Specifies the scope of termination and uptake of dependencies.

≠

Responsibilities disappear

Renaming does not automatically erase old obligations or history.

Explanatory task

Answers conceptual or evidential questions.

≠

Choice task

Requires the corresponding complete set only when comparison and proposed options are requested.

Teaching construction: applicability of six categories in one fictional queueTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe values, capacities, and observation period are all teaching constructions, with no actual service deployment. The original processing capacity 1 is an existing service; inaction does not cancel it.

A fictional service queue has backlog 6 at t=0, 2 arrivals per hour, and existing processing capacity 1 per hour; compare the next two hours. Explicit inaction preserves the original service without adding resources, yielding endpoint 8. Active maintenance adds 1 processing unit per hour to preserve backlog 6. Active improvement adds 2 per hour to the original 1, for total processing 3 and endpoint 4. Delay uses the original processing 1 in the first hour and, after approval, increases it to 3 in the second, taking the backlog to 7 then 6. A small trial increases processing to 2 in the first hour with monitoring, then handles the second hour under a predetermined rule. Exit or transfer is marked inapplicable because there is currently no verifiable receiving party; transfer capacity is not invented. Every additional option remains only a candidate.

BoundaryResource costs and actual authorization have not been compared. Endpoint 4 being smallest does not justify declaring immediate implementation necessary. The trial's second hour still depends on observations and cannot be treated as a fixed endpoint.

Mathematical construction: natural depletion reveals the difference between maintenance and inactionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDepletion, inputs, and the linear update I_next=I−2+replenishment are stipulated assumptions; no actual experiment was conducted.

A purely technical fictional inventory starts at 10, loses 2 naturally each period, and has no other existing inputs. Adding no replenishment for two periods yields 8 then 6. Actively replenishing 2 each period preserves 10 then 10, but requires total additional input 4. Saying the latter option “does not change final inventory” does not mean it “involves no action or cost.”

BoundaryActual inventories may involve thresholds, demand, and protection obligations. This pure construction should not be used to infer duties of care for people or organizational responsibilities.

Teaching construction: an auditable inaction baselineTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe observation rules and responsible role are teaching templates only; no work has been assigned to any actual person.

Inaction record for the queue above: baseline t=0, B=6; expected values 7 at t=1 and 8 at t=2; check arrivals and actual completions hourly; reopen option review if any complete record shows B≥7; fictional duty role R observes and records. Reopening is only review and does not automatically increase processing resources. If records are missing, mark unknown and trigger a material review; do not treat missingness as low risk.

BoundaryActual responsibility must be accepted by a qualified actor with the capacity, time, and permissions. This template cannot establish that anyone has taken it up in reality.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleMaintaining the status quo and inaction both ultimately seek stability, so combine them.

What it limitsMaintenance may require continuous additional input, while the inaction baseline may deteriorate. Distinguish them by actual actions and resources.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleAll six categories must be listed, so mark transfer feasible even without a recipient.

What it limitsChecking six categories does not make six options feasible; missing uptake should be marked inapplicable or awaiting evidence.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleEven explaining one concept requires six action options.

What it limitsWithout a request for choice, no action list is mandatory; the task determines output scope.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • An inaction baseline must not presume that existing obligations stop or that costs are absent.
  • Clearly inapplicable options must not be invented to fill the form.
  • Small steps, delay, maintenance, and exit can all have high-impact consequences; names do not guarantee safety.
  • Avoid double-counting a combined option's resources and benefits; candidate options are not execution authorization.

Scope and open questions

This section explains option generation and baseline status. Explicit constructions hold conditions constant for the same object, avoiding presenting historical practices as genuinely available options when complete permission and resource records are absent.

  • Material on actual costs, permissions, service uptake, and low-power positions is absent; the demonstration options do not constitute a real-world optimal recommendation.

Why does inaction in the queue yield a backlog of 8 rather than keeping it at 6?

Existing processing is 1 per hour and arrivals are 2, giving a net increase of 1 each hour: from 6 to 8 over two hours.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

What additional conditions are needed to maintain 6?

Increase processing to 2 per hour, adding 1 unit per hour with separate resources, authorization, and protection conditions.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

How should exit be recorded when there is no receiving party?

State that it is currently inapplicable or lacks evidence of uptake; do not fabricate a feasible transfer.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

What is the minimum record required for inaction?

Baseline time, expected path, observation plan, reopening conditions, and responsible party, while preserving existing obligations.

12.10A Common Card for Comparing Options ​

In briefA unified comparison card unifies questions, baselines, and obligations, rather than forcing every value into one total score. Whether information helps, whether actions jointly qualify, and whether resources support them simultaneously are three questions requiring separate proof.

Compare each option against the same baseline. Record at least the option description, forecast reference, normative premises, people affected, rights floors, expected path, worst acceptable outcome, cross-circle spillovers, distribution of costs and benefits, value of information, risk of lock-in, reversibility, resource costs, implementer, authorization, stopping, rollback, and remedy.

Dimension of ComparisonQuestionWhat Cannot Substitute
Target and pathWhich path is the option intended to change?An abstract promise to “make things better”
Protection floorWho might suffer unacceptable harm?Average benefit
DistributionWho benefits, who pays, and when?The aggregate net value
Cross-circle spilloversDoes local improvement externalize costs?Metrics from the primary circle
Value of informationCan the option distinguish mechanisms or paths?The dramatic character of the action itself
Reversibility and lock-inIf it goes wrong, can it be stopped, reversed, or remedied?Verbal promises
PermissionsWho may decide, execute, and appeal?A model’s suggestion or a job title
No actionWhat path will unfold if nothing is done?An assumption of zero cost

If options cannot be compared on a single scale, retain the outcomes on multiple dimensions and disclose the conflicts. Do not force them into a sum. Conflicts among value premises should be handled by qualified subjects and procedures. The model should fully show where conflicts arise and what their consequences are. It may offer a preference and reasons for deliberation under openly stated normative premises. It cannot make a binding final decision in place of a qualified subject.

The value of information can be written as a limited formal object. Let a denote the action, θ the state, Z the information, and U the utility accepted in advance. Then EVSI=E_Z[max_a E(U|Z)]−max_a E(U). EVSI is nonnegative when Z is free to obtain and can be ignored, and when the action set and objective remain unchanged. Actual investigation has costs in time, privacy, and resources. It may miss a window or change the available actions. Its net value should be counted separately. Two clues may change the action only if both are obtained. The value of understanding can exist independently and need not all be converted into this quantity for decision-making. 〔Studies 07.08, formal statement of conditions〕

12.10Note

Understanding this section

12.10 Unified option comparison card

A unified comparison card unifies questions, baselines, and obligations, rather than forcing every value into one total score. Whether information helps, whether actions jointly qualify, and whether resources support them simultaneously are three questions requiring separate proof.

Compare each option against the same baseline, target, and deadline. Minimum records include the option description, foresight references, normative premises, affected parties, minimum rights protections, expected path, worst acceptable outcome, cross-circle spillovers, cost-benefit distribution, information value, lock-in risk, reversibility, resource costs, executors, authorization, stopping, rollback, and remedies. “Large benefits and controllable risks” alone provides no reviewable comparison.

Targets and paths must state which mechanism changes. The protection floor must identify unacceptable harm; average benefits cannot substitute for it. Distribution must state who gains, who pays, and when; an aggregate net value is insufficient. Cross-circle spillovers require checking whether costs are externalized; indicators for the main circle cannot monopolize evaluation.

Information value asks whether new observations distinguish mechanisms or paths, or change an evidence-based choice, rather than whether an action is dramatic. Reversibility and lock-in ask whether stopping, withdrawal, and remedy are actually possible; verbal promises are insufficient. Permissions must identify who can decide, execute, and hear appeals, and within what valid scope; a job title or model recommendation is insufficient. Inaction still follows a changing baseline and cannot be assigned zero cost.

Without a reasonable common unit and public trade-off rules, multidimensional results should retain vectors, conflicts, and rankings under different normative premises. A model can explain which option it favors under disclosed norms and what would change that judgment, but cannot make a binding final decision for qualified actors. Forced summation can hide minimum rights protections or silently set interpersonal utility exchange rates.

The bounded information-value formula is EVSI=E_Z[max_a E(U(a,θ)|Z)]−max_a E[U(a,θ)]. Here θ is the state, a the action, Z the information, and U a previously accepted utility with a computable expectation. The formula compares the optimal expectation when the action can respond to Z after learning it with the optimal expectation from choosing one action without Z. Utilities and probabilities need declared status; a conditional model calculation is not a verified real-world benefit.

Nonnegativity requires information to be free and ignorable, with the action set and target unchanged. If the original optimal action remains available after information is acquired, one can do at least as well as before. Actual inquiry takes time, privacy, and resources and may change the object or make actions expire, so gross EVSI is not net value. Unquantified privacy and rights costs cannot default to zero, nor may they be forcibly monetized just to use the formula.

Two clues may each leave the decision unchanged yet be valuable together, so information values need not add up item by item. Knowledge also has value for understanding independent of this action; EVSI=0 in this formula does not make research worthless. Section 12.10.1 further explains when a common action is feasible under uncertainty; 12.10.2 checks shared resources across multiple actions. The parent section's comparison card cannot replace these two tests.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Complete comparison fields for the same baseline, target, and deadline, retaining each burden-bearing position.

  2. 2

    Without a reasonable common scale, retain multidimensional results and disclose normative conflicts and conditional preferences.

  3. 3

    For information value, first specify states, signals, actions, and utility, then state the calculation's conditional status.

  4. 4

    Prove gross information value nonnegative when information is free and ignorable and the action set is unchanged; separately deduct corresponding real-world costs.

  5. 5

    Check clues' joint effects, commonly acceptable actions, and shared resources before submitting the choice to a qualified procedure.

Distinctions to keep clear

Unified comparison

Itemized records under common questions and baselines.

≠

Unified scalar

Possible only with additional justified trade-offs and conditions on units.

Gross EVSI

Expected gain from allowing choice after information within a fixed model.

≠

Net value

Also includes inquiry time, resources, privacy, and opportunity costs.

Zero decision information value

The information does not improve choice for the given target and actions.

≠

No knowledge value

Values such as understanding can exist independently.

Conditional preference

Reasons for deliberation under explicit norms.

≠

Final binding decision

Requires qualified actors and valid procedures.

Mathematical proof: nonnegativity of bounded EVSITeaching scenario

AssumptionsA finite probability model, finite action set, and integrable utility are explicit conditions. This is an algebraic argument, not a real-world experiment.

Assume a finite, nonempty, fixed action set and existing utility expectations; take the no-information optimal action a*. For each signal z, max_a E[U(a,θ)|Z=z]≥E[U(a*,θ)|Z=z]. Taking expectations over Z and applying the law of total expectation gives the left side ≥E[U(a*,θ)]=max_a E[U(a,θ)]; subtraction yields EVSI≥0. Being free and ignorable ensures that feasible strategies after the signal still include the fixed a*. If the action set changes, this step may fail.

BoundaryNonnegativity concerns gross expected value. It does not show that every specific signal improves matters, guarantee positive net value for real-world collection, or establish permission.

Mathematical construction: two individually unhelpful clues are valuable togetherTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll distributions, utilities, and costs are stipulated; no information was actually collected.

Independent fair bits X and Y have four combinations, 00, 01, 10, 11, each with probability 1/4; state θ=X XOR Y. Action a∈{0,1} scores 1 for a correct guess and 0 otherwise. Without information, θ is uniform and the best expectation is 1/2. Observing only X or only Y leaves the other uniform, so the expectation stays 1/2 and each individual EVSI=0. Observing X and Y together allows exact calculation of θ, scoring 1 every time, so joint EVSI=1−1/2=1/2. If the two pieces of information cost 0.6 in total on the same utility scale, with nothing else changing, net value is 0.5−0.6=−0.1.

BoundaryThis does not imply that real-world information can always jointly resolve ambiguity. Cost comparability is also stipulated; actual privacy and rights constraints cannot be arbitrarily converted.

Teaching construction: multidimensional comparison without forced summationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe options and effects are constructed; no actual user data is described or collected.

Fictional option A reduces waiting by 2 hours but adds privacy exposure; option B adds no exposure but reduces waiting by only 1 hour. Without public privacy constraints and time trade-offs, “2−privacy points” should not be disguised as an objective total score. Report waiting, whose information is exposed, difficulty of withdrawal, the protection floor, and resources separately; then exclude A under an explicit premise that specified additional exposure is prohibited.

BoundaryExclusion follows from the explicit constraint, not automatically from the numerical time values; compare again if the evidence changes.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleEVSI is nonnegative, so inquiry is worthwhile however expensive it is.

What it limitsNonnegativity concerns only the gross value of free, ignorable information; real-world net value can be negative.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleX and Y each have zero EVSI, so their joint EVSI must be zero.

What it limitsIn the XOR construction, they jointly reveal the state exactly, giving a gain of 1/2.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleIf no total score can be calculated, no preference can be proposed.

What it limitsA conditional preference can be offered for deliberation under explicit norms, retaining conflicts without overstepping authority to decide.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • The maximization formula does not turn utility premises into natural facts or automatically authorize information collection.
  • If information is not free and ignorable, gross EVSI's nonnegativity cannot establish that real-world inquiry is always beneficial.
  • Two individually useless clues need not be jointly useless; information values generally cannot be mechanically added.
  • Complete comparison-card fields improve reviewability only; they do not certify factual accuracy or real-world permissions.

Scope and open questions

Formal information value here is most directly tested by a complete proof and enumerable construction. Without a real project's full utility, probability, cost, and permission material, no empirical EVSI is fabricated.

  • Acceptability of actual utilities and probabilities, comparability of privacy costs, and permission to collect information require separate material and procedural judgments.

The optimal action after the signal is at least as good as retaining a*; then apply the law of total expectation.

Why does observing only X give no gain in the XOR example?

Y remains fair, so θ's conditional distribution remains 1/2 for each value; X alone cannot raise the expected success of guessing.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

What is the net value when cost is 0.6?

Gross value 0.5 minus cost 0.6 gives −0.1, assuming cost and utility are comparable.

Basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Why need a unified comparison card not produce a unified total score?

Dimensions may be incommensurable or subject to hard rights constraints. Unified recording is sufficient; trade-offs require additional public reasons.

12.10.1From Identifiable Answers to Feasible Choices ​

In briefNot knowing which state holds need not prevent all action; yet each state having its own solution does not ensure that one common qualified solution can be selected now.

A question can have a sufficient answer while action remains infeasible. There can also be a commonly acceptable action before all states have been identified. For each state z compatible with the available material, let A_ok(z) denote the actions acceptable under the disclosed minimum protections, resources, and valid permissions. In a finite, single-round deterministic choice, if the intersection ∩ A_ok(z) is nonempty, the common options can be compared without first distinguishing all states. This gives one condition under which bounded action is possible while unknowns remain. If the intersection is empty, “there is a solution for every state” is insufficient to establish that the right one can be chosen now. Check whether obtaining more evidence, waiting, narrowing the task, or taking a protective action with independent grounds could change the conditions.

The intersection concerns only the credible states listed and the explicit constraints. It does not guarantee that unknown states will never arise. Risk probabilities, costs, or normative tolerance can support other choice rules, but they must be stated explicitly. The worst-case criterion must not be concealed as the only rational one. Permissible randomized or sequential strategies must also be analyzed separately for their respective objectives. The single-round condition above does not rule them out.

12.10.1Note

Understanding this section

12.10.1 From identifiable answers to feasible choices

Not knowing which state holds need not prevent all action; yet each state having its own solution does not ensure that one common qualified solution can be selected now.

Let the credible-state set compatible with current material be nonempty. For each state z, A_ok(z) is not an arbitrary imagined list, but qualified actions determined by public targets, protection floors, resources, and valid permission. Otherwise even a nonempty formal intersection contains only paper actions, not real feasibility.

In a bounded single-round deterministic choice, a nonempty common intersection means at least one action qualifies in every listed compatible state. These shared actions can then be compared without first identifying the actual state. This is a positive condition for bounded action with unknowns, not a requirement to wait indefinitely for perfect knowledge.

If the intersection is empty, each set separately being nonempty is insufficient. Knowing z1 would select left and z2 right, but a current representation that does not distinguish them cannot guarantee the right selection with one deterministic rule. Check whether further evidence, waiting, a narrower target, or independently grounded protective actions alter conditions; do not assume those options automatically available.

Conversely, a sufficient answer does not guarantee action. Even if z1 is identified, inadequate resources, failed protection, or missing permission may leave A_ok(z1) empty. Identification, computability, access, implementation, resources, and authority to adopt carry different responsibilities; a correct answer is not a pass for all.

The condition covers only listed credible states and constraints, without guaranteeing no omitted states. Nor does it declare worst-case criteria uniquely rational. Grounded probabilities, risk tolerance, randomization, or sequential strategies may yield other rules, but must state their own targets and conditions rather than extending this single-round deterministic result without bounds.

This matches F3 in §4.18.3 (Chinese source lines 1017–1020) and Appendix C.12 (lines 4603–4607). The comparison card first defines qualification; this section proves whether a common action exists under limited information. The next tests whether multiple shared or separately feasible actions compete for one resource.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    List a nonempty credible-state set compatible with current material, without claiming unknown states exhaust reality.

  2. 2

    For each state, first check targets, protection, resources, and permission to form A_ok.

  3. 3

    Compute the common intersection, publishing its members or emptiness and their bounded meanings.

  4. 4

    A nonempty intersection permits comparison of shared options; emptiness prompts checks of further evidence, a narrower task, or independently grounded strategies.

  5. 5

    Retain the single-round deterministic domain without excluding separately grounded probabilistic or sequential methods.

Distinctions to keep clear

Each state has a solution

Every A_ok(z) is separately nonempty.

≠

One common solution exists

The intersection of all sets is nonempty, a stronger logical claim.

State sufficiently identified

The actual current state is known.

≠

Action feasible

Resources, protection, and permission must also hold.

Commonly qualified

Meets constraints in every listed compatible state.

≠

Absolutely safe in reality

Unlisted states and changing conditions may still occur.

Single-round deterministic condition

One action qualifies for all stated states.

≠

All decision theories

Probabilistic, randomized, and sequential strategies have their own analyses.

Formal proof: common action is equivalent to a nonempty intersectionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA bounded single-round deterministic task, nonempty observation class, and already determined qualified sets.

Necessity: if the same action a is chosen using only current representation y and qualifies for every compatible z, then a∈A_ok(z) for every z, so a belongs to the intersection. Sufficiency: if the intersection is nonempty, take any a in it; a qualifies for every z without identifying the actual z. The proof uses only set definitions, not evidence of real qualification of each set.

BoundaryDoes not prove necessary/sufficient conditions for sequential, randomized, or risk-tolerant strategies, or certify actual permission.

Teaching construction: a common protective option under unknown stateTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAction names, states, and authorization are formal stipulations; no actual preservation action occurs.

Fictional z1 has qualified set {left,preserve}, z2 has {right,preserve}; preserve is assumed to have this task's resources, protection, and valid authorization. The intersection is {preserve}, allowing comparison and selection without knowing z1 versus z2. If preserve's permission expires and it leaves both sets, {left} and {right} remain with empty intersection. The previous version's feasibility no longer applies.

BoundaryPreserve is not a magically lawful action; failed premises require rechecking.

Formal construction: knowing the answer may still leave no feasible actionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsCapacity and constraints are stipulated; no actual resource request is made.

Material uniquely identifies z1, but required action left needs capacity 2 and only 1 exists; all other actions violate stipulated protection constraints. A_ok(z1)=empty, so the state is fully identifiable while the task cannot be executed. Only actual additional capacity and satisfied permission may create a new qualified set.

BoundaryKnowing the resource shortfall does not mean new resources have arrived or the old cutoff automatically extends.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleEvery state has an action, so the right action can certainly be selected now.

What it limits{left} and {right} are separately nonempty but their intersection is empty.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleSince not every state is known, all bounded action must stop.

What it limitsIf an already qualified common action exists, identifying every state is unnecessary.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleAn empty intersection proves randomized and sequential strategies useless.

What it limitsThis condition does not address them; analyze their respective targets and constraints separately.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • Do not place unauthorized actions in qualified sets and then use the intersection to prove authority.
  • An empty intersection does not prove every form of action or strategy impossible.
  • Additional observation may involve cost, risk, and permission; it is not automatically available for free.
  • A nonempty intersection establishes common candidates, not a uniquely optimal action already chosen or executed.

Scope and open questions

This is a formal proposition; complete set proofs and boundary constructions are more appropriate than incomplete real material presented as permission and feasibility certification.

  • Actual state-set coverage, qualification constraints, and permission still require case-specific evidence; only the formal relationship is verified here.

12.10.2Joint Feasibility of Multiple Options ​

In briefEach task may claim to need just one resource, ultimately promising the same resource twice. Joint feasibility must put capacity, dependencies, personnel, stopping capability, and deadlines into one constraint table.

When several actions are feasible individually, also check whether implementing them at the same time would draw on the same capacity, budget, staff, and stopping channels. If two units of service must both be completed in the current period and it has capacity for only one unit, each is feasible on its own but they are infeasible together. Added capacity next period cannot recover a deadline already missed in this period. Adding capacity in the same period or adjusting the deadline with adequate grounds and authorization can yield a new feasible option. It must not be used to rewrite the old task as completed.

Joint comparison should therefore account for resource use, task dependencies, and key deadlines together so different departments do not commit the same resource twice. Parallel work shortens waiting only when conditions allow. Where investigation, authorization, implementation, and taking effect depend on one another in sequence, they must still follow that order. Treating completion of the first node as proof that the last affected person is already protected misjudges both timing and coverage.

12.10.2Note

Understanding this section

12.10.2 Joint feasibility of multiple options

Each task may claim to need just one resource, ultimately promising the same resource twice. Joint feasibility must put capacity, dependencies, personnel, stopping capability, and deadlines into one constraint table.

Individual feasibility establishes completion when an action uses conditions alone, not enough capacity, budget, personnel, or stopping channels for simultaneous execution. Departments passing separate reviews still need joint-constraint checks if they use the same resource. Differently named resources may depend on one underlying person or platform.

The minimal counterexample has two unit tasks, each occupying the whole current period and both due by its end, with capacity only 1. Each alone needs 1≤1 and is feasible; together they need 2>1 and are infeasible. Additional capacity next period does not change this period's deadline; later completion is not timely completion of the original task.

Adding same-period capacity changes constraints. A grounded and authorized extension of one deadline can also create a feasible new option, preserving the original contract and revision status. If the old deadline was already missed, later successful completion does not erase the late record. Scheduling mathematics cannot erase delay harms or protections for affected people.

Resource scheduling also needs task dependencies. If premise verification, authorization, execution, and effect have serial dependencies, tool concurrency cannot make them all complete simultaneously. Actually independent reads or tasks may run in parallel, but shared write targets, common capacity, version prerequisites, and conflicts need handling rules.

Stopping capability is also a resource. If one person or channel cannot respond to several stop requests within the critical window, separate stopping promises cannot simply become joint stoppability. Rollback, remedy, and monitoring may compete for the same resources and must be checked alongside normal execution.

Task completion must reach the promised affected people and protective outcomes. First-node completion, sending a request, or interface success does not mean the last person is protected; check timing and coverage together. This connects to the end-to-end clock in 12.6, with the unit-capacity counterexample in Appendix C.12, Chinese source line 4601, directly supporting the formal boundary.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    List each action's resource use, dependencies, deadline, and actual completion endpoint.

  2. 2

    Find shared underlying resources, personnel, and stopping channels, checking capacity jointly for every period.

  3. 3

    After individual feasibility, separately check joint inequalities; conflicts prohibit repeated promises of the same resources.

  4. 4

    Same-period expansion or lawful condition changes create new options; old deadline results are not rewritten.

  5. 5

    Check serial critical paths, endpoint coverage, and stopping/remedy capability; first-node completion does not replace whole-task completion.

Distinctions to keep clear

Individual feasibility

An action using resources alone meets constraints.

≠

Joint feasibility

All actions satisfy shared constraints together under one schedule.

Later resource replenishment

More may be done in the future.

≠

Original deadline met

Required sufficient resources and actual completion at the time.

Independent parallelism

No prerequisite dependency and sufficient resources.

≠

Forcing serial work into concurrency

Executes downstream work before its premises hold.

Execution capability

Normal action has resources.

≠

Stopping and remedy capability

Simultaneous exceptions also require resources and actual mechanisms.

Mathematical construction: two current-period tasks compete for one unit of capacityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsDiscrete single period, indivisible unit workloads, and stipulated capacity/deadlines.

Tasks A and B each need one full unit of current-period capacity and are both due at period end, with C1=1. Separately, dA=1≤1 and dB=1≤1; jointly, dA+dB=2>1, so both cannot finish on time. If current capacity becomes 2, demand 2≤2 can be scheduled. If only next-period capacity rises to 2 while both original deadlines remain, current-period tasks still cannot be met.

BoundaryDivisibility, different durations, or preemption would change the model; those conditions cannot be silently inserted into the original.

Mathematical construction: a lawful new deadline permits a new scheduleTeaching scenario

AssumptionsGrounds and authorization for extension are explicitly assumed in the construction; no real extension occurs.

Continuing the example, suppose a valid procedure changes B's deadline to the end of period 2, with C1=C2=1. Schedule A in period 1 and B in period 2: each period uses 1 and meets the new respective deadline. Feasibility of the new contract does not complete the old contract requiring both this period; if lateness already occurred before revision, it remains.

BoundaryReal delay may harm a party, still requiring applicable protection, rights, procedure, and remedy judgments.

Teaching construction: stopping promises also conflict over resourcesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPersonnel, operation duration, and simultaneous signals are teaching constructions, not descriptions of a real safety system.

Two fictional pilots run simultaneously, each requiring the same supervisor to perform a manual shutdown taking exactly 1 minute within 1 minute of receiving a stop signal. If both signals arrive together and no other stopping channel is available, one supervisor cannot perform both at once. Individual stoppability does not establish that joint operation meets the same stopping deadline.

BoundaryReal systems may have independent automatic stopping or multiple personnel; verify these rather than assume they exist.

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleA and B each pass individual resource review, so joint implementation also passes.

What it limitsShared resources may be promised twice; check constraints under a common schedule.

Teaching counterexampleAdding capacity next period proves this period's deadline was not missed.

What it limitsFuture resources cannot restore a past deadline; at most they support catching up and a new option.

What does not follow

  • Joint-feasibility proofs depend on actual stipulated demand, capacity, and deadlines; mathematics does not certify these inputs.
  • Extensions require grounds and valid procedures; models cannot rewrite contracts themselves.
  • Shared resources include personnel, budgets, and stopping channels as well as machine capacity.
  • A feasible schedule is neither completed execution nor delivery of promised protection to affected people.

Scope and open questions

This section's common-capacity counterexample follows directly from public constraints; no actual resource and deadline files were obtained, so actual organizational breaches or protection failures are not invented.

  • Divisibility, parallelizability, resource capacity, stopping delays, and effective deadlines of actual tasks still require evidence.

Why are demands of 1 each individually feasible but jointly infeasible under capacity 1?

Individually 1≤1, jointly 2>1; the same original deadlines do not permit borrowing from another period.
